pages.title: Aetheria at a glance
pages.summary: The whole app in brief: the three destinations, the Workshop, a story and its modes, the Observer, and the words the app uses.

figures.alt: The welcome to a new archive
Maelis beginning the first tour of the house

blocks.text: Aetheria is a place to write stories and roleplay with AI characters, passage by passage. It runs as a desktop app and on Android phones. The replies come from the model providers you add keys for in Workshop → Providers, or from a model running on your own computer.
Getting around

On a desktop the rail down the left holds the three destinations, Table, Stories and Library, and below them "Search" (Ctrl K, or Cmd K on a Mac), "Workshop", "Import", "You" and "?" (your guide, the guide). On a phone the bar along the bottom holds Table, Stories, Library, Workshop and "More" (Search, Import, You, your guide, and the current workspace's index).

items: Table: where stories begin. Draw cards (characters, lorebooks, worlds) from the archive drawer onto the bench; what is on the table is in the story. "Just begin" (or "Begin with these") starts it, "Continue" (with the story's name) returns to the last story, "Begin a campaign" starts a game-mastered one. On a phone the three read "Begin", "Continue" and "Campaign".
Stories: the shelf. Every story bound as a volume with its chapters; open, pin, rename, export or delete them.
Library: everything you own, in decks. Story objects: Characters, Lorebooks, Worlds. Authoring: Presets, Memory. The Studio, reached from the Characters deck, makes a character by interview.

Workshop: the settings, in rooms, each listed with what it is doing now ("On · every 4 of your turns", "OpenRouter · …"). How it works: Memory, Observer, Providers (keys and models), Image, Voice, Plugins. The app: Appearance, Reading, Archive, About.

Import: one door for character cards, chat exports, lorebooks, presets, personas and world packages. It works out what a file is and files it where it belongs; a chat becomes a story with the character you choose.
You: who you play in the open story (with no story open, it opens your personas).

? (your guide): ask how anything works, or take a tour ("Show me around", "A story’s page", "The map", "The world", "A campaign", "Your first story"). Tours are scripted and make no model call; questions use your own model. Their own page (The guide) says what they is sent and what a question costs. A new archive comes with a starter set, Lantern Quay: two characters, their lorebook and world, and a storytelling preset, which the first tour has you set out on the table.

blocks.text: When you leave a story for the Library, the Workshop or the Studio, a "Back to" chip at the top returns you to it; its ✕ ("Put this away") hides it.
A story

Its head shows the name, the context gauge (tokens the next request will use, out of the model's limit; press it to inspect the assembled request), an estimate of what the next reply costs (press it for the breakdown), the model chip (choose the model this story writes with; the choice also becomes the model new stories start with, and the one the Observer and your guide answer with) and "The story" (its Details: cast, chapters, notes, tools). The chevron at the end of the head folds it away ("Collapse story header"), and the one in the tab row brings it back. The tabs below are Chat, Map, World (when "Worlds in stories" is on, or the story has a world: off, it says so and offers "Turn worlds on") and Campaign (only in a campaign). The chapter path runs along the bottom.

items: Chat: the manuscript and the composer.
Map: every chapter, passage, take and branch, and planned beats.
World: the story's world, its map, its people and what has changed.

blocks.text: The Story Index on the left lists, in order, what the story sends the model. It starts closed: open it with the "Story Index" door or Ctrl+B. On the right, the inspector has the tabs Details, Observer and (with a world) World.

The Observer is a second reader beside the story. It answers about the story and never writes into it. your guide is the default Observer, and its panel has two hats: "The story" (talk about what you are writing) and "The app" (ask how Aetheria works). On a desktop it opens from the composer's Observer button or Ctrl+O; on a phone from the story's "Tools".
The words the app uses:

items: Passage: one written turn in the chat, yours or a character's.
Take: one version of a reply. Asking again makes a new take; every take is kept, and the arrows under a reply ("take 2 of 3") move between them.
Branch: a take that was carried on, so the story continues differently from that point. The map shows the branches.
Beat: only a planned beat, something planned ahead on the map before it is written.
Chapter: a story is bound in chapters. Closing one seals its summary, and the story carries on in the next.
Story: the whole thing, with its chapters, cast, preset, lorebooks, memory and, if you want one, a world.
Binding: a theme. Gilt & Slate is the default.

blocks.text: What costs a model call: every reply or new take is a request to the story's model; with story tools on, one reply can take up to three. Other things make requests of their own, among them story memory, the Observer, building a world and keeping it up to date, a chapter summary you ask to have written, the stewards, the Studio, a campaign's recap and your guide's answers (one request a question, up to three when they looks a page up). Each page here says what its feature calls. Reading, browsing the map, moving between takes you already have and opening the Story Index cost nothing.
Phone and desktop

On a phone, side panes become sheets that rise from the bottom; a story's head has "Index" (or swipe in from the left edge) and "Tools" (Change model, Assembled context, The story, Play a side scene, Observer). Keyboard shortcuts are for a keyboard: press ? to see them all.

pages.title: The Table
pages.summary: Where a story begins or resumes: draw cards onto the bench, choose who you play, then Begin, Just begin or Continue.

figures.alt: The Table with Dilys, Ansel and the Lantern Quay lorebook on the bench

blocks.text: The Table is the first destination in the rail (on a phone, the first tab along the bottom): where a story is begun or picked up again. It has the bench, where cards are laid, and the archive drawer beneath it. Its rule: what is on the bench is what is in the story.
The head
On an empty bench it reads "A clear bench" ("Draw a card from the shelf, or just begin"); with cards down, "What is on the table is in the story". Its controls on a desktop:

items: "You play": who you will play (below).
"Continue <story name>": only once some story is started (a passage written or someone cast); it opens the chapter you touched last. The Table lists no stories; that is the Stories shelf.
"An idea from your guide" (desktop, only with "What you enjoy" switched on in Workshop → About): your guide suggests three things to make, from the lines kept there (see "What you enjoy").

"An opening from your guide", once the bench holds more than one character besides the one you play, or one with a lorebook or a world: your guide writes one opening from everything on the table (the characters, lead first, who you play, the lorebooks' entries and the world's book), in their panel. "Begin with it" there begins the story from this bench with it as the first passage (the lead's own openings stay as other takes); see Making things with your guide.
"Begin a campaign": a sheet that makes a new story of its own and leaves the bench alone (see the Campaign page).
"Just begin" on an empty bench, "Begin with these" once cards are placed.

blocks.text: On a phone: the title, then "You play" across the screen, then "Continue", "Campaign" and "Begin" side by side ("Opening", for "An opening from your guide", takes Continue's place while the bench has what it needs).
Drawing

The drawer ("Draw from the archive") holds your characters, lorebooks and worlds (not presets), with "Search the archive" (names and tags) and tabs All, Characters, Lorebooks, Worlds. Worlds are there only while "Worlds in stories" is on (Library → Worlds); with it off the Worlds tab is empty. Click a card (or Enter) to set it on the bench, or drag it onto the bench to put it where you let go; let go elsewhere and it goes back. On a phone the drawer is a bar ("Archive drawer", "N cards ready to draw"): tap to open, then tap a card, or drag it upward (sideways scrolls the drawer); it closes once a card is placed. On a phone the cards are drawn smaller, on the bench and in the drawer: three sit side by side in a row, and a card drawn takes the next place in the rows rather than covering another. The open drawer keeps to about a third of the screen: "Search" and a picker for which cards ("All", "Characters", "Lorebooks", "Worlds", each with its count) share one line in place of the tabs. On a laptop's short window (768 pixels tall or so) the drawer's cards are drawn smaller, so the bench keeps room.

On the bench, drag cards anywhere; the arrangement is kept on this device. Drag one off the edge, or focus it and press Delete, to take it off ("Undo" puts it back); arrow keys move a focused card. Double-click a card to open its deck in the Library. Faint threads join a lorebook to its character and a world to every character. Cards on the empty bench wait there until you begin.
Beginning
"Just begin" (or Ctrl+N, Cmd+N on a Mac, from anywhere) opens an empty story. "Begin with these" makes it from the bench:

items: The characters become the cast, except the one you play. The first character placed (other than the one you play) leads: the story takes their name and opens with their greeting, their other greetings kept as takes. With two or more characters, the lead's group-only greetings come first. A greeting's {{user}} becomes whoever you play (or your usual character, or your name), and its other card macros are filled in, as when a story starts from a character's card.

Lorebooks on the bench are switched on, for the whole story. A character's own lorebooks come onto the bench with them, set down beside their card and joined to it by a thread; lift one off to leave it out.

A world becomes the story's world (one only, the first placed), used while "Worlds in stories" is on. Placed while it is off, a notice says the world waits until worlds are turned on in the story's World tab.

blocks.text: Beginning calls no model; the first reply you ask for is a request to the story's model.
Who you play

"You play" offers your usual character, marked "(as usual)", if you have one; "No one in particular"; each character on the bench; and, under "Your personas", your personas (played without being on the bench). "As usual" seats them even if their card is not on the bench (set who that is under "In new stories" in the You panel). A bench character can be chosen only when two or more are there: the AI needs someone to play.
A story on the table

"Lay out on the table" (in a story's menu on the Stories shelf, or on its page) puts an existing story on the bench: its cast with whoever you play, its lorebooks and its world. The head reads "On the table" and "Changes here change the story": a card placed joins the story at once, a card taken off leaves it ("Their passages stay"). Taking off the character you play leaves you playing no one. "You play" here is a true swap: whoever you played goes to the AI, unless that would leave the AI no one ("The AI needs someone to play."). Buttons: "New bench" (the empty bench), "Begin a campaign" (a new story beside this one) and "Back to the story"; on a phone "New", "Campaign", "Story".

pages.title: The starter set: Lantern Quay
pages.summary: What comes with the archive: Dilys and Ansel of Lantern Quay, their lorebook, world and preset; setting them out, playing either, getting them back.

blocks.text: A new archive comes with a starter set, put in while the welcome is read, with no model asked:

items: Two characters of Lantern Quay, a cold harbour town that grinds the lenses for every lighthouse on the coast. Dilys Pengelly, 27, the salvager, who owns whatever the tide brings in and has taken to diving for it. Ansel Truscott, 29, the young master grinder whose lens is in the sea. They sat the same exam at twelve and have been at odds since; whether that stays a feud is up to the story.

"Lantern Quay", a lorebook: the Works, the Tideright, the wreck of the Constance, the people of the town. Each character has it as their own. The town itself is always on; every other entry fires on its keys as whole words ("inn" is the Tidewater Inn, never "dinner") and stays for that reply and the two after it.

"Lantern Quay", a world with a map: the Quay, the Tidewater Inn, the Works, Gull Rock and its causeway, the moor. Built on the device. Bringing it in turns "Worlds in stories" on, because the drawer only shows worlds while it is on; a world is only in a story when its card is on the table.

"Aetheria Storyteller", the house preset, written for collaborative fiction in small blocks that each do one thing: never writing your character for you (nor hearing what they only think), people who know only what they have seen, voices from their own lives, facts that stay facts, prose tested against its own draft, no echo of your last line, twelve choices (whose eyes, how you take part, how long, how fast time moves, the mood, how the world treats your character, who drives the story, how romance moves, whether people change, talk or telling, how long consequences last, how far it may go) and tones to mix. In a new archive it is the one new stories use. Presets has the whole of it.

blocks.text: The story

The finished lens for a new lighthouse at Cape Morrow went into the sea when the barge Constance capsized. Its 312 numbered prisms are washing up one at a time, and by the Tideright, a charter older than the harbour wall, whatever the tide leaves is Dilys's to sell, and she has started diving the wreck to get there first; Ansel designed the lens and has to buy it back. The Board wants the lens in forty days or the town's work goes inland, Dilys owes her fee at quarter-day, and someone in hobnailed boots reaches the beach first. Nothing is decided in advance; the lorebook names who the bootprints could belong to and leaves it to the story.
Who you play

On the Table, "You play" chooses. Play Dilys and Ansel is waiting at her shed with a list of numbers when she comes up out of the sea; play Ansel and she is on the strand with three of his prisms already labelled. Play no one with both on the table and they are both in it, at the Tidewater Inn, and you are a stranger who has found a prism nine miles from the sea. Each card also has another opening as a second take.
Setting them out

After the welcome's tour of the house, your guide sets them out with you: open the drawer, put Dilys, Ansel, the lorebook and the world on the table, choose Dilys or Ansel to play, Begin. They waits for each; "Do it for me" does that step, "End the tour" stops. For who you play they suggests one of the two, with a word on what each is walking into, and waits until you choose one under "You play" ("Play Dilys" and "Play Ansel" choose for you). "No one in particular" is still in the list, but the tour goes on only once you play one of them. If the house tour is skipped they offers the setting-out on its own.
The first session

After Begin, your guide goes into the story with you and sees you through its first session, still waiting for each thing you do: choose a model (passed over when the story already has one), see that its provider has a key on this device, write your first line and send it, read the reply as it arrives, ask for another take, open the Story Index (and see where memory lives), open the Map and come back to Chat, open them as the Observer, and open "New chapter" to look (nothing is ended). "Do it for me" on the first line puts in a line for whoever you play (answering the other's opening), to change or send; the reply has no "Do it for me", since it is your model writing. The reply and the other take are each one request to your model; the rest asks nothing.
The key and a failed reply

When the story's provider has no key on this device, your guide says so before your first line, naming the provider: "Show me" opens Workshop → Providers with that provider chosen and points at where the key is pasted; once it is saved, "Back to the story" returns you (a provider that needs no key, the custom proxy or one on this computer, is passed over). If a reply or a take fails anyway (a refused key, no connection, a model the provider will not serve), they says what went wrong in plain words and offers "Try again", with "Show me where" (Providers) or "Choose a model" when that would help. Your passage stays in the story, so the composer is left empty.
On a phone

Tools comes first, then the Observer inside it, each waited for; the sheets the tour opened are put away before "New chapter". While the reply arrives they steps aside to a small tab at the edge of the screen, so you can watch it come ("Show" brings them back), and the step that says to read the opening leaves the page lit. Finishing it counts as the tour of a story's page, so that one is not offered again. The last step names their other tours, under "?" (More on a phone). It can be run again from Workshop → About, "Set the table with your guide"; their tours there and in their help panel list it as "Your first story" while any of the set is in the archive.
Getting them back

Workshop → About, "The starter set": "Bring in Lantern Quay" for an archive that never had it (an archive from before it is told once, on the Table, by the "New in 1.5" card: "Bring them in and set the table" brings the set in and starts the setting-out), or "Put back what is missing" for a piece that was deleted (a deleted world is noticed only while "Worlds in stories" is on). Bringing it in there never changes which preset new stories use. They are ordinary cards, each with its portrait (picture cards, so they export as themselves), a lorebook, a world and a preset: edit, rename or delete them like any other.
Their pictures

The lorebook (a salvager's ledger by lamplight), the preset (an open book under gilt stars) and the world (the town on its cliff across the harbour at dusk) each come with a picture on their card, and the world's shows across the top of its Now. An archive that had the set before the pictures gets them once, by itself. A part given its own picture keeps it, and a picture taken off ("Picture", then "Take it off", or "Take it off (show the map)" on the world) does not come back; "Add a picture" puts one on again from your files.

pages.title: Stories
pages.summary: The shelf of every story, each a volume bound with its chapters: open, pin, rename, lay out, export or delete.

blocks.text: Stories is the second destination in the rail (on a phone, the second tab along the bottom): the archive of everything you have written. Each story is a volume on the shelf, with its chapters bound inside.
The shelves

On a desktop the Index on the left lists four, each with a count of stories: "All stories", "Pinned", "Multi-chapter" and "Standalone" (one chapter). On a phone they are tabs. They are fixed; there are no folders of your own. Above the volumes: "N on this shelf", the shelf's name, and a line on what the archive holds (stories, chapters, passages, how many are yours), with "Search stories" (chapter titles, story names and tags; a volume then shows only the matching chapters) and "New", which begins a blank story and opens it.

A volume shows a cover (the lead character's portrait), "Single thread" or "N chapters" (with a search, "2 of 5 chapters" or "Chapter 3 of 5") and when it was last touched, the name, who is in it, its passage count, and "pinned". The most recently touched comes first. A story nobody has started (no passage, no cast) is not listed, except the one open now; side scenes are listed with their story, not on the shelf.
Opening

Click a cover to open the story. On a desktop one click on the title selects it and shows its page on the right ("This story"); double-click or Enter opens it. On a phone one tap opens it. A story of several chapters lists them beneath (number, title, passages, when); each opens the same way. The story's page is the same one "The story" opens inside a story: counts, "Continue", "Open the map", "Lay out on the table", its name and "What it is about", cast and world, what memory holds ("People and places", "Lately", "Everything remembered"), the chapters with their sealed summaries, its side scenes, "The story as it stands", "Show the scene card" and its tools, "Run this story as a campaign…", notes and "Delete story" (see The story's Details).
The story menu is the "⋯" beside a volume's title:

items: "Continue", "About this story" (its page; a sheet on a phone), "Open the map", "Lay out on the table" (onto the Table's bench), "Rename story…", "Pin" or "Unpin".

"Export story as a book (PDF)" (desktop app only), "Export story as a book (EPUB)", "Export story as a book (web page)" (instead of PDF on a phone), "Export story as Markdown", "Export story as text", "Export story as JSON".
"Delete story".

blocks.text: A chapter row's own "⋯": "Open", "Rename chapter…", "Export chapter as Markdown", "... as JSON", "... as text", "... as PDF" (a web page outside the desktop app), "... as EPUB", "Delete chapter".
Finer points:

items: A story is pinned as a whole: "Pin" marks it, and "Unpin" lets go of it, whichever chapter was pinned. The Pinned shelf shows pinned stories with all their chapters.

A book has a title page, the cast and each chapter in order: the path each chapter took, not every take, each passage under whoever wrote it, without the trackers and markup passages carry for the model. Markdown and text of a story are the path taken too; its JSON holds every chapter in full. A chapter's own Markdown or text is different: it begins with the chapter's system prompt and lists every passage it holds, takes you did not follow included, as "You" and "Assistant". Side scenes are not exported.
With a story open, the command bar (Ctrl+K) offers "Export this story" (every chapter, as Markdown).

Delete asks first ("This cannot be undone."; a story of several chapters says how many go). A story's side scenes go with it, and a chapter's with that chapter. Chapters go one at a time; if one cannot be deleted it stops there, says so, and offers "Try again".
"Rename story…" changes the name all its chapters share; "Rename chapter…" changes one chapter's title.
Nothing on the shelf calls a model.

pages.title: The Library
pages.summary: Everything you own, as cards in five decks: Characters, Lorebooks, Worlds, Presets and Memory. Read a card, then unfold its editor.

blocks.text: The Library is the third destination in the rail (on a phone, the third tab along the bottom). It holds everything you own as cards, in five decks, and opens on Characters. On a desktop the Index on the left lists the decks in two groups, each with a count:

items: "Story objects": "Characters" (Who enters the story), "Lorebooks" (What the story knows), "Worlds" (Where the story lives).
"Authoring": "Presets" (How it is told), "Memory" (What is remembered; its count is the stories that remember something).

blocks.text: On a phone the deck's name at the top is a menu for changing deck. Each deck has its own page in this guide. Memory is not a shelf of cards: it opens straight into the memory workspace.

The head shows the deck's name and how many cards are shown, with "Import" (opens Intake, see Importing), on Characters "Make one by interview" ("By interview" on a phone; the Studio, where a character is made by answering questions) and "Make one with your guide" ("With your guide" on a phone; your guide makes one with you in their panel, see "Making things with your guide"), on Presets "Make one with your guide" too, and "New character", "New lorebook", "New preset" or "Make a world". New makes a blank character or lorebook ("New preset" starts as a copy of the Default Preset, the house preset) and unfolds its editor at once; "Make a world" opens the world workspace and switches on "Worlds in stories" (the switch at the top of the Worlds deck).

The shelf line on a desktop: "Search <deck>" (names and tags), "★ Favourites" (not on Worlds), the order ("Recent" or "A–Z"), the deck's tags, and the layout, "Deck" or "Grid". Favourites always come first. On a phone: the search and "Filter", which opens "Filter the shelf" (Favourites only, Order, Marks, Lay out as, "Show every card"). Each deck remembers its layout; Presets and Lorebooks start as a grid.

The deck is a fan of overlapping cards that opens under the pointer and rests open at its centre card. Drag it sideways, or push the pointer into either end, to travel; on a touch screen the cards lie whole and you flick. Its foot reads "01 of 12", with ‹ and › to step through, and "← → Browse · Enter Open · Space Choose · F Flip". Beneath, the chosen card is read (or, until you choose, the one at the centre): its name, description (a preset says how many prompts are switched on), tags, "Unfold editor", on a character "Rebuild by interview", and on a lorebook, preset or world "Add a picture". In the grid the reading appears once you choose a card.
A card's picture

A character's card shows its portrait (changed in its sheet). A lorebook, preset or world can have a picture too: "Add a picture" under the card chooses one from your files (PNG, JPEG, WebP, GIF, BMP or AVIF). It is made smaller to fit the card, about 768 by 1152, and kept inside the object, so it goes with it when the lorebook or preset is exported or the world is shared. While it is being saved the button reads "Saving the picture…". With one on, the button reads "Picture" and offers "Choose another picture…" or "Take it off" (on a world, "Take it off (show the map)"); taking it off shows "Picture taken off", with "Undo" to put it back. Without a picture a lorebook or preset shows its initials in gilt, and a world shows its map. A world's picture also heads its Now room in the world workspace, with the same "Picture" button there. Nothing is sent anywhere; no model is asked.
A card:

items: Click (or Space) chooses it; double-click (or Enter) opens its editor.
"Flip" turns it over to its back: kind, name, entries or prompts, when updated, up to three tags ("Unmarked" if none). "Front", F or Escape turns it back.
The star on its front marks a favourite.

blocks.text: The editor is the object's sheet. It unfolds out of the card over the Library; Escape or Close folds it back. What each sheet holds is on that deck's page.
Came here from a story? A chip at the top, "Back to <story name>", returns you; "Put this away" (the ×) dismisses it. It shows in the Workshop and the Studio too.

A deck that cannot be read says so ("Nothing has been deleted.") and offers "Try again". Browsing and making a blank object call no model; what an editor or the Studio sends to a model is on its own page.

pages.title: Characters
pages.summary: Character cards and their sheet, imported cards (PNG, CHARX, JSON), who you play, the cast of a group story, portraits and the living character.

blocks.text: Every character is a card on one shelf, Library → Characters. Any card can be played by the AI in one story and by you in another. Personas (below) are the one exception to the shelf: they are yours, kept in You, not in the Library. Make one with "New character", "Make one by interview" (the Studio) or "Make one with your guide" ("With your guide" on a phone), or bring one in with "Import". Open a card with "Unfold editor" (or "Open full editor" in the Story Index, or "Character sheet" beside a portrait). The sheet saves itself a moment after you stop typing; "Save" forces it; Escape or "Close" folds it back.
The sheet's sections (a "Page" picker on a narrow screen):

items: "Identity": "Name", "Display name", "Tags" (Enter adds one; click a tag to remove it).

"Portrait & motion": "Still portrait" (the card art, used in the Library and exports): "Choose image", then "Replace image", takes a PNG, JPEG, WebP, GIF, BMP or AVIF. An optional "Motion portrait" (MP4, WebM or MOV) loops silently and wins over the still wherever motion is shown: "Add video", "Replace video", "Remove video". A still portrait can be replaced but not removed. The Live card's "Change portrait & motion" opens this section.
"Personality": "Description", "Personality", "Creator notes" (never sent to the model).
"Living pages" (below). "Scenario". "Greetings": "First message" and "Alternate greetings". "Example dialogue" (exchanges separated by <START>).

"Voice": the voice their lines are read aloud in, one per speech engine, kept on the card so it travels with an export. Empty means the narrator's voice; "Hear it" plays a sample. The engine in use comes first; "Voices for the other engines" shows the rest.

"Advanced prompting": "System prompt" and "Post-history instructions" (the jailbreak slot). With a list-builder preset these replace the preset's Main Prompt and Post-History Instructions blocks unless the preset forbids it; {{original}} inside them brings the preset's text back.
"Group behaviour": "Talkativeness" and "Group-only greetings".

"Metadata": "Creator", "Version", "Source", and the exports "PNG card (v2)" (it holds the v3 card as well, so other apps, which read the v3 one first, show the card as you left it), "CHARX (v3)" (on the desktop it carries the motion portrait) and "JSON". An export carries the card alone: not where its picture is kept on this device, its favourite star or its collections. Its lorebooks go with it: the ones it is bound to here are written into the card as its own book (character_book), as they are now, edits and all, every entry with where it goes and its settings, and the card imported again (here, on another device or in another chat app) brings them in as its book. Two or more go as one book, under the first one's name and settings (its token budget among them); one deleted since is left out. A card bound to no lorebook here carries the book it came in with, if any. Its voices and living pages go with it.

blocks.text: The right column, "Live card", has "Begin a story", "Rebuild by interview" and "Delete character" (stories keep their passages).

Greetings: a story begun from the card opens with the first message, and each alternate greeting is another take of that opening passage. your guide can write a new one for a card ("An opening", see "Making things with your guide"): kept, it joins the alternate greetings (one written for several characters on the Table joins the lead's group-only greetings). On the Table, with several characters, the lead's group-only greetings come first, and its first message and alternate greetings follow as further takes. {{user}} in a greeting becomes whoever you play.

Imported: a PNG, CHARX or JSON card keeps its fields, tags and extensions, including its regex scripts (they then run on that character's passages). An embedded lorebook (character_book) is offered as "Import Lorebook?"; "Import" files it and binds it to the character. Importing a card already on the shelf offers "Update it" (see Importing).
Who you play

Story Index → "You" (eyebrow "In this story"; also the rail's "You", and "Play as…" in the composer's ✦ menu). Its card, headed "You play", names who: a character, or "No one in particular", when the box beneath is what the story calls you (your name in every story where you play no one; it is kept as you type). An opening nobody has answered yet follows it: give your name, or step into someone, before the first reply and the opening says that name instead of "User". Playing a character, the card holds "Description" (folded, with how many words; a change there changes their card, in every story) with "Open full editor" inside it, and "Play no one in particular". Below it, "Your personas" (see Personas). Then "Step into someone" lists everyone the AI plays, each with "Play" and "The AI plays them."; while you play no one, or with "Hand … to the AI when you swap" off, the last one the AI has says "The AI plays them, and needs someone to play." and cannot be taken. "Someone from the Library…" opens "Search the Library" to play anyone not in the story yet, and "Browse the Library". A swap is a true swap: "When you swap" folds to its answer ("They stay, played by the AI" or "They leave the scene"), and inside it "Hand <name> to the AI when you swap": on, whoever you played stays in the scene played by the AI; off, they leave it. The AI always needs someone to play. Earlier lines keep who wrote them; from the next reply, {{user}} is the character you play and the preset's persona slot carries their description and personality. "In new stories" folds to who you begin as ("You begin as no one", or their name); inside it, "Play <name> in new stories" makes them who you start as ("Start new stories as no one in particular" while you play no one). The composer then asks "What does <name> do?".
Personas

A persona is a name and a few lines about who you are, kept in You rather than in the Library: Story Index → "You", under "Your personas", or the rail's "You" with no story open (a sheet, "Who you are"). They are not in Library → Characters, the Table's drawer or "Add a character"; on the Table, "You play" lists them under "Your personas". Each has "Play" (or "Playing") and "Open", which unfolds "Their picture" ("Choose a picture": shown beside your passages in every story where you play them), "Name", "Who you are" (sent as who you are, in any story where you play them; written as you like, with {{user}} for you and {{char}} for the character the AI plays), "Play <name> in new stories", "The full card" (the character sheet) and "Delete persona" ("Delete" or "Keep them"; stories keep their passages). "New persona" asks for a "Name", "A picture" if you like ("Choose a picture"), and "Who you are", then "Make the persona". Playing a persona sends what a persona always sent: {{user}} is their name and the persona slot carries who they are. Made a character, their words are turned to a card's own voice ({{user}} becomes {{char}}). Under every persona, "Make <name> a character" offers the step up, since a character can do more (an opening, a personality, a voice, and the AI can play them too): "Fill them out with your guide" (they reads them back, asks a few questions and writes the rest, keeping what you wrote; a few requests on the model you make things with; see Making things with your guide) or "As they are" (into the Library with nothing written). Either way it is the same card, so every story with them keeps them. Personas from older versions were turned into characters; those nobody ever filled out (no opening, personality or example dialogue) are personas again. Import reads persona backups from other chat apps into You (see Importing).

The cast is Story Index → "Characters". To bring someone in, use "Add a character" at its foot: "Search the Library", then press a character ("Add"); with two or more the story is a group story. Their own lorebooks come into the story with them (a notice names them, with Undo), on for the whole story. With two or more: "Speak now" (one passage from them, now), "Quiet" (in the scene, answers only when asked), and behind "⋯": "When it isn't their turn, the others see" ("Full", "Name only", "Hidden"), "Talkativeness", "Move earlier", "Move later", "Play <name>" and "Remove" (with Undo; passages stay), also the × beside each name; the last character can be removed too, and the narrator then tells the story alone until someone is invited. Whoever leaves is listed under "Earlier in this story" with "Bring back". "Secrets they know" ("Only theirs" or "Every secret", for a narrator or game master) is there for every character. "Who answers": "Whoever is addressed" (default: anyone named answers, others join by talkativeness), "One at a time", "Everyone, in order", "Only when I ask", and "Told together" (one reply per send, told as one scene, in which whoever the moment needs speaks; one request instead of one for each character). The line above the composer shows who answers next and picks someone for one send; @name addresses a character, and in "Told together" a chosen or @named character answers alone. Except in "Told together", every reply is its own call to the story's model, so "Everyone, in order" costs a call per character per send; but everything before the story is the same whoever speaks (the preset speaks of the cast as a whole, and every card the others may see is set out under its name, with its personality and how it speaks), so after the first reply the provider can read most of each request back from its cache (see Providers, "Saving money"). Who answers is said after the story, with what only they carry: their description when the others see only their name or nothing, their card's own instructions, and their living page. A passage told together is the narrator's: it carries the cast's names, shows the portrait of whoever it names first, and its memory knows every secret, marked as one.
The living character

Switch on "Living document" and the character keeps a living page over its card (self-understanding, beliefs, relationships, goals, boundaries, current condition, contradictions) that wins where they disagree. "Document scope": "This story (default)" or "The character card" (follows it into every story, written only from takes the story carries on from, never swiped-away ones). "Revises itself": "In the moment" (a hidden receipt at the end of each reply), "On reflection" (the memory pass revises it between scenes) or "Both". "Awareness": "Immersive", "Self-aware", "Authorial / meta-aware". "May amend the story" lets it edit the story's living canon. While on, the page rides in every request after the description (more tokens, no extra call); off, nothing is sent. The Story Index's "Living character" row has the same switch for whoever speaks next.
Portraits

Clicking a character's portrait on a passage opens it beside the story ("In this scene", "Character sheet", Close) while you keep reading and writing. A motion portrait plays on hover; expression images, if the character has any, show as thumbnails after "Default". On a phone it is a full-screen layer. Leaving the story closes it.

pages.title: Lorebooks
pages.summary: Lorebooks (world info): entries that join the request when their keys come up, how they fire, and which books a story uses.

blocks.text: A lorebook (also called world info) is a volume of entries. An entry's text is sent only when it activates, usually because one of its keys came up in the story. Lorebooks live in Library → Lorebooks: "New lorebook" makes an empty one, "Import" takes a lorebook or world-info JSON, and a character card's embedded lorebook (character_book) is offered when the card comes in. The other way, a character's own lorebooks go out inside its card when the card is exported, as they are now (see Characters). "Unfold editor" opens the lorebook sheet. A lorebook's card can have a picture: "Add a picture" under it in the Library (see The Library); it is kept in the volume and goes with it when exported.

The sheet: the entries on the left ("Add", "Search entries"; each row shows its title, first keys, "always on", "either list" or "with secondary keys" when it fires so, "outlet" and its name for an outlet entry, and its tokens), the chosen entry in the middle, and "When this fires" on the right. With no entry chosen, the right side holds "Volume name", "Export volume" and "Delete lorebook". "Export volume" writes the volume as a JSON file: on a desktop it asks where to save it, on a phone it goes to Downloads (or Documents, or the share sheet when those cannot be written), and the sheet says where. The sheet saves itself; "Save now" forces it. "Remove entry" has an Undo. On a phone the entry list is under More → "Sections" (or swipe in from the left edge); in windows narrower than 1180 pixels the right side is a drawer that opens when you choose an entry.
An entry:

items: "Title": for you, not sent. "Content": what is sent.
"Keys": with commas between them; a key is a word or a phrase the story might write (several words are fine). A key written as /pattern/flags is a regular expression.
"Secondary keys": used as "When it fires" says.

"When it fires" (on the right): "Always" (sent with every request, keys or none); "On a key" (any of its keys; the secondary keys are not used; where a new entry starts); "On a key from either list" (any key, from the keys or the secondary keys); "On a key and any secondary key"; "On a key and every secondary key"; "On a key, with no secondary key"; "On a key, unless every secondary key is there". The last four are the logic other chat apps use; "either list" is Aetheria's own, and an exported book writes such an entry's keys as one list, which fires the same way there.
"Case sensitive", "Whole words only", "Disabled".

"Where it goes" (on the right): "Before the character" (where a new entry starts), "After the character", "Before the example dialogue", "After the example dialogue", "Before the author's note", "After the author's note", "In the history, at its depth", or "Outlet", which shows "Outlet name" (see Outlets, below). These are the places other chat apps use, so an exported book reads the same there.
"Insertion order": activated entries are sent lowest first.
"Depth", and "Use probability" with "Probability" (the chance it goes in when it activates).

blocks.text: How it fires, and the gotchas:

items: Each reply, the story's books are searched in the latest passages (four by default) and the system prompt built for the reply; the story memory recalled for it is not searched (it changes every reply, and lore it set off changed with it). A key that appears in the system prompt fires its entry every time.
With a world bound to the story and worlds on, where the story is now is searched too, so an entry keyed on a place comes in while the story is there.

Only an entry that is always on is sent without a key. Every other entry needs one of its keys in what is searched (or, for "either list", a key from either list), then whatever its secondary keys ask; an entry with no keys at all is never sent unless it is always on. (Before 1.6.1, an entry made in the sheet, and many a card's book, was sent with every reply whatever its keys.)
For an entry at the usual place, "Depth" is how many of the latest passages are searched for its keys. Only an entry placed at a depth (@D, from an import) is inserted that far back in the history.

Imported sticky and cooldown values are honoured: an entry with sticky 3 that fires on its keys stays for that reply and the two after it, then needs its keys again (before 1.6.2 an entry kept on by sticky started its turns again and never went off). Recursion (one entry's text triggering another), which some imported lorebooks expect, does not run; instead an entry marked as another's child comes in with its parent, up to three levels deep. The sheet does not set either.

A book can carry its own token budget (token_budget, which many shared books and card books have; the sheet does not set it). Then at most that many tokens of its entries go into one reply: an entry kept on by sticky first, then the highest "Insertion order". One that does not fit is left out, and a smaller one after it may still go in; an entry that came in with its parent goes only if the parent did, and one marked to ignore the budget always goes in. Each book keeps to its own budget; there is none across books.

blocks.text: Where it goes. An entry that is always on (and anything it brings in with it) lands where it asked: with a list-builder preset (as imported chat-completion presets are), at the preset's "World Info (Before)" or "World Info (After)" block (a new entry made in the sheet goes before), or around the example dialogue. An entry that fired on its keys goes inside the story instead, two passages from the end, just before story memory, whichever of those places it asked for: such entries change from one reply to the next, and before the story they stopped the provider reusing the rest of the request from its cache (see Providers, "Saving money"), so the whole story was paid for in full every reply. Entries placed at a depth (@D, from an import) or around the author's note go into the history where they asked. Lore costs only its tokens: it rides in the story's own request, with no extra model call.
Outlets

An entry whose "Where it goes" is "Outlet" is sent nowhere by itself, as in other chat apps: its text is filed under its "Outlet name", and goes only where a preset's block, a character card's field or a preset's format string writes {{outlet::that name}} (the name is read without the spaces at its ends). Every entry that fired under one name goes there together, lowest "Insertion order" first, one line apart; an outlet nothing fired under, or a name no entry has, gives nothing. It stays where the macro is even when it fired on its keys, so an outlet written before the story changes the request there whenever it does (see Providers, "Saving money"). An outlet entry still counts against its book's token budget; one with no name is never sent, and its row says "outlet with no name". Both preset builders read {{outlet::name}}. An imported book keeps its outlets (a card's book keeps each one's name too), and an exported book writes them back as it found them. In the Story Index an outlet entry that fired counts among "lore entries switched in", and its text counts with the block that places it; "Context preview" shows it under "Lorebook" by its outlet's name.

Which books a story reads: those attached in Story Index → "Lorebooks" ("Add" or "Remove" under "Attach", or the × under "In this story", which also takes out a book that came with the character), plus every character's own book (one bound to the card when it was imported, or one your guide made for them). A book an older archive sends with every story says "sent with every story" in the Story Index and cannot be taken out of one story. Every one of them is on for the whole story, whoever is speaking: an entry is sent when its keys come up. A character's own book comes into the story with them: "Begin a story" from a character attaches it, "Add a character" in the Story Index brings it (with Undo), and on the Table it is set down on the bench beside the character. On the Table a lorebook is in the story while it is on the bench; lift it off to take it out. The "Lorebooks" row also has "Quick edit": choose an "Entry" (among the first 40) and change its text there, to test it in the next reply; the change goes into the lorebook itself. "The chapter so far" row counts the lore entries switched in.
Lore links

Workshop → Reading → "Lore links in the manuscript" (off by default) underlines words in passages that match a key of an entry in the story's books; hovering one with the mouse shows the entry's title and text. A touch screen has no hover, and clicking a link does nothing yet. Very large lorebooks switch the underlining off.

pages.title: Worlds
pages.summary: A world for the story to be set in: its map, worldbook, people and changes; opt-in, built locally, and what it costs.

figures.alt: The map of Lantern Quay, with the route panel beside it

blocks.text: A world is a place for a story: a map, a worldbook of what is true there, its people and where they are, and a record of what changed. Its engine is built in and works offline. Worlds are opt-in: nothing of one is used until "Worlds in stories" is on, and only in a story that has a world.
The Worlds deck

Library → Worlds holds your worlds. Its switch "Worlds in stories" (once called Veils) "Adds World mode to stories, with the bound world's context, map and living state." Opening a world or "Make a world" turns it on; the Story Index's World row has the same switch. Off, no world is sent, and your worlds are not read at all. A story that has a world still shows its World tab, which says the world is off and offers "Turn worlds on"; a story without one has no World tab while it is off. Off, the Worlds deck can say "No worlds yet", and the Table's drawer and "Begin a campaign" show none. Turn it on and they are all there again; nothing is lost. A world's card shows its map, or a picture you give it ("Add a picture" under the card; see The Library), which travels with the world when it is shared. A world with a picture also shows it across the top of Now, as a wide strip (not beside the story, and not over the map); "Picture" there chooses another or takes it off. A wide picture suits it best: the card shows the middle of it, the strip its whole width. Until you first move in a world, a story's World tab opens on "The world is built. Take your first step." with "Open the map" (opening the world at the top of the shelf when the story has none open) and "Dismiss".
Making a world

"Make a world" opens the Book: describe the place in prose and press "Build the world". That is one request to the model for worlds (the story's own, unless you chose another under "Everything else": see Providers), which names the places in the book and how they sit to each other (the harbour on the shore, the inn halfway up the cliff path, the moor inland); it never gives coordinates. The engine then lays out the land on your device with no more calls: the coast, cliffs, rivers, roads and areas, and each town's streets, squares and houses round the buildings the book names. The same book lays out the same world every time. "Draft the structure only" makes the request without building. "Copy the prompt" lets you use any model: paste its answer into "The structure", then "Build from this structure" (no call). When it is built, a note says so by name (and that the story now takes place in it, when one is open). Where the book did not say where something is, it is placed sensibly and the note says "Placed by guess" with its name. Lines of the book the world cannot show are kept as unresolved. your guide can also make one with you from a line or two, in their panel ("Make something", then "A world"): they asks a few questions, writes the book and draws the map, and the world waits for "Keep the world" (see "Making things with your guide").
From a lorebook

Under the Book, "From a lorebook" reads one of your lorebooks ("This story's lorebook", "This story's lorebooks (2)" with more than one, or any from the shelf); it is there only when you have a lorebook. With no world yet, "Build a world from it" writes both the Book and the world in one request; "Write the book only" writes the Book and the structure to read over first. With a world, "Add it to the book" writes what the lorebook says about places into the Book (one request), for you to read and then rebuild. "Fill in what it leaves out" (on by default) lets the model place what the lorebook names without saying where, and add the ground, water and roads between, never a new town or person. Only entries about places are read when a lorebook is long; the note says how many were left out. The lorebook itself is never changed.

The Book is the world. Change the Book and press "Rebuild from the book": the model is shown the book before and after and proposes only what the edit implies, shown as a revision to "Apply revision" or "Cancel".
Worlds made before maps were drawn this way are still built the older way until rebuilt from their book.
The rooms: Now, Map, Worldbook, Changes, Making.

items: The head: on Now, "The world", its name and one line on how it stands ("Paused · Day 1, 00:00 · told to this story"; from the Library, "told to the story you were last in"; "not told to this story" when "Tell the story about this world" is off; "no story open" when none is), then the rooms. On Map and Worldbook the name and the rooms share one row, so the page has the height. "Undo the last world revision", "Redo the world revision", "Refresh worlds" and "Close" stay at its end; in a story, "Beside the story".

Now: "Waiting for you", when changes wait, with "Review them". "Where things stand": with nobody placed, "Place yourself" (and "Open the map"); once you are placed, where you are and who else is in the world. "Who is here" (you first, then who is here, travelling, resting or missing, and where) and "Lately", with the world's clock and weather and "The whole record". "The land": the world's description. Beside them, "In your story": "Tell the story about this world" (on by default; where you are and who is near go with each reply, up to 1,200 tokens by default: tokens, not calls), "Notice what the story changes" (on by default; with the story's memory pass, at no extra request), "Apply routine changes by themselves" (on by default: moves, events and finds go straight on, each with Undo in the record; a new place, an owner or damage still waits; no extra requests) and "Life in the background" ("Paused", the default, "With the scenes", "Now and then, while open", "Steadily, while open"; the engine's own steps, no model asked). "Move the world on once" takes one such step by hand (no model); "More of what is told" opens "What the story is told, and how", in Making. With no story open, "In your story" says each story sets how its world takes part.

Map: the map fills the page. Drag, wheel or pinch, or the zoom buttons ("＋", "−"); "View", "Edit", "Fit", "Party", "Layers" (the "Map layers" to show or hide), and a search ("Find a place, character, pin, or event…"). "The land" shows the whole world and "The town" goes to its main town; the closer you are, the more is drawn (a town as a mark from afar, then its streets and houses). "Gilt chart" and "Parchment" are the two looks; the choice is kept. Pointing at a spot says what is there and where (on the moor, in the town, the sea 300 m west), the place's own description, and what the story's lorebooks say about it: entries whose keys name the place, or its town. A chosen spot offers "Plan travel here" and "Open Worldbook". "Edit" lets you drag a place you set down (Shift chooses more than one), then "Review move", with "Undo move", "Redo move" and "Cancel". Beside the map, a drawer with three tabs, "Travel", "Shape" and "About", folds away with its arrow to a strip at the edge (press the strip to open it again); where the window is narrow it sits under the map. "Travel": "Who moves" ("You", or "Someone else…": tick who goes under "Who goes", you too if you go with them, and "Track …" puts someone from the story's cast on the map), "Where to" (a place by name, a way and how far such as "2 km north", or coordinates) and "By" ("Walking", "Riding", "Sailing", "Flying"), then "Preview the route", which shows the distance and the time ("Where exactly?" when a name could mean more than one place, each offered), then "Travel" or "Cancel"; the world's clock moves on by the time the journey takes. "Shape" is shaping by hand (below). "About" says how to work the map, what it could not place, and the land. Beside a story the map has no drawer: under it, where you are, and "About the map".

Worldbook: one row for the search ("Search names, other names, tags and text"), "Every kind", "Every region", "More filters" ("This timeline only", "Show archived entries", and the order: "By name", "Recently changed", "By importance") and "New entry". The entries stand on shelves by kind (Settlements, Regions, Ages…), each with its count; the ones the map made itself (river meetings and the like) are folded together as "Made by the map", and a count over the shelves says how many those are. An entry opens on its name, "In a line" and "The whole entry", with the rest folded, each showing its value: "What it is" (name, "Kind", "Truth": "Canonical fact", "Rumour" or "A character's knowledge", "Importance"), "Who may see it" ("Public (the story may use it)", "Private", "GM only"; only public entries are sent), "On the map" (where it is placed), "Other names and tags" ("Also called", "Tags") and "Where it came from" (how sure, its revisions, relationships, and "Merge another entry into this one"); then "Save the correction", "Lock", "Archive" and "Show on the map". Under the shelves, "The worldbook in the story" has "Let the story consult the worldbook" (on) and "How much it may send" ("Balanced · 360 tokens" by default, from "Lean · 180 tokens" to "Deep · 700 tokens"). Lorebooks (world info) are a separate deck.

Changes: what the story proposed, with evidence and how sure it is: "Apply", "Edit" or "Ignore", or "Apply all" and "Ignore all" when several wait. "The record" keeps every decision with its reason, with "Undo the last revision". When the world is not noticing, "Let the world notice the story" turns it on. "How the story is read" holds the settings below, "Read the current scene" and "Advance the world once"; "Per kind of change" sets each kind to review, auto or ignore.

Making, in three folds. "This world and others": your other worlds, "Import a world…" and "Export this world…", and "Delete this world…". "The book of the world": the Book, "The structure" and the built world as data. On a phone the Book's box is half the screen tall; "Open it in full" (under it, once something is written) makes it as tall as the text, to read down the page, and "Fold it back" returns it. "What the story is told, and how": "Tell the story about this world", "What it tells" (eight kinds of detail, each on or off), "How much, and how strictly" ("Everything the world may send": "Lean · 600 tokens" to "Deep · 2,400 tokens", "Balanced · 1,200 tokens" by default), "Exactly what is sent" ("Build the preview" shows the world's part of the next request word for word) and "Unlink from this story" (the world stays in the library).

blocks.text: Shaping by hand

Open "Shape" in the drawer beside the map and press "Draw on the map". Choose "Place" (one click; a second click moves it), "Draw" for a road or river (two points or more) or "Region" for an area (three or more), and its "Kind". In a world drawn this way the kinds are the map's own (an inn, a smithy, a ford; a track, a river; a wood, a moor, a lake). Click the map ("Undo point" and "Clear points" help), give it a "Name", then "Review this edit". Every change is a revision to "Apply revision" or "Cancel", and "Undo revision" at the head of the world takes one back. What you set down stays where you put it, a building in a town is joined by its streets, and a line about it goes into the Book: "Accept the wording" is chosen; "Use my edit" takes your own words, and "Change the world only" or "Reject the wording" leaves the Book alone. "Towns" chooses how a town is laid out, then "Review this change": "Laid out from the book" (streets, squares and houses round the places the book names, with anything you set down added) or "Only what you place" (the town begun again from scratch: its named places, what you set down, and the lanes between them). "Manage" works on the places you set down by hand ("Authored place"): change the "Name", "Also called", "Description" or "Tags" and "Review edit", or "Duplicate" or "Delete" it. Older worlds also have "Paint", "Water" and "Sculpt", and for a place or a road or river, "Settle it onto the terrain" (on by default): ticked, a new place, or the point a road or river's name sits at, is moved to good ground nearby; unticked, nothing is moved. None of this calls a model.
Sharing a world

Under "Take this world out", choose the "Package" ("Full built world" keeps the built land as it is; "Recipe only" travels light and rebuilds it exactly), the "Story history" ("Leave it out", the default, or "Include it"; what you wrote in the worldbook, the map's entries you archived or corrected, and any entry you locked, as it stands and still locked, even one the story made, go either way), "Private and GM-only entries" ("Leave them out", the default, or "Include them"; left out, nothing of them goes, not their text in earlier versions or in the story history either; a place on the map whose entry is private or GM-only stays off the shared map too, with what stands in it (a town's buildings, an island's tower and its land), and its name and description go from the book, the worldbook, the pins and the story history; a road or river that led to it or was named for it keeps its line without the name, and an atlas world's preview is drawn again without it), an "Author" and "Include a preview image", then press "Export this world…"; nothing is published anywhere. "Import a world…" checks the file and shows what it holds before anything is added, and says when it "Contains private or GM-only worldbook material": "Add to the library", "Keep as a copy" or "Cancel"; when a world with the same identity is already here, "Replace the existing one" or "Merge histories" (from a file without its story history, the story here is kept and the file's worldbook entries are added to it; from a file without its private and GM-only entries, those here are kept, and so are the places it left out, as they are here). "Delete this world…" asks first; stories that used it keep every passage, and on the desktop its files go to the Recycle Bin.
What noticing costs

Changes → "How the story is read" → "When": "With memory" (the default) uses what the story's memory pass already found, no extra call, so story memory must be on. "After every reply" and "After each scene" each make one request to the model for worlds (the story's own unless you chose another; see Providers) after every reply. "When asked" waits for "Read the current scene" (one request). What each of these requests cost goes on the story's cost ledger (Story Index → "What this story has cost"), as "The world noticing". "Review": "Automatic by policy" (the default) applies routine changes it is sure of (0.8 and above, set in "Automatic above") and never anything destructive; "Suggest changes" makes everything wait for you; "Manual only" stops the story proposing anything. "Minutes per tick" and "Changes per tick" set how far each step of the background life goes. Side scenes never change the world.
Places the story finds

A place the passages name that the world does not know comes to Changes: in a world drawn as a map, "… was found, and set on the map", pinned where the passages put it, by the places they name ("on the moor, north of the Teeth"). When they do not say where, it is "not on the map yet". The pin belongs to this branch of the story; the map itself is not changed. On the map such a pin says "found in the story", and "Read it in the story" opens the passage it came from (in the story's World view, or beside the story).
Branches and the world

Each branch of takes has its own world. Choose another take on an earlier passage and the world is as it was before that passage (who was where, what was found, the clock); go back to the first take and its world is as you left it. A new chapter goes on from the branch the one before it ended on. Delete the story's newest passage and what it changed in the world is taken back with it; a passage deleted from the middle leaves the world as it is. Worlds from before this kept no record of when things changed, so their branches begin from the world as it is.
In a story

The Story Index's World row chooses the world. The World tab is the whole world, opening on Now; with no world yet it offers "Worlds" (choosing one gives it to this story) and "Book". On a desktop, the map button by the tabs ("Keep the world beside the story") or "Beside the story" keeps Now and the Map in the inspector's World tab as you write. A selected passage whose scene names a place offers "Open in the World". The "Travel in the world" story tool lets the model move the party; asked for a place the world does not have, no one moves and the model is told the places it does. In the world, the reader is the party, "You", never a new person. When a story first opens in a world, its cast is set out where they belong: at the place whose description names them, else a place their card names, else the main town. When the story's lorebooks are read for a reply, where the story is counts as named, so entries about that place come up without it being said in the chat.

On a phone the World tab works, in one column, but cannot be kept beside the story; the rooms' names share one line in a smaller type (with a large text size they wrap to two), and the map's buttons scroll sideways. A pinch on the map zooms around the place between your fingers; lift one and the other drags.
The guide's tour

The first time a world's rooms open, your guide offers "The world": the rooms, the land and the town, the two looks, pointing at a place, travel, shaping by hand, the switches on Now, the Book and a world from a lorebook. Each room opens as they gets there. Workshop → About has it as "The world".
Gotcha: in the Library a world acts for the story you were last in. Opening a world's card makes it that story's world; "Make a world" leaves that story without one until the new world is built.

pages.title: Presets
pages.summary: Presets: the house preset and its choices, the prompt chain, sampling, dials, panels, display scripts, own styles, request fields, import and export, macros, and quick edits from the story.

blocks.text: A preset is how a story is told: the ordered chain of prompt blocks sent with every reply, and the sampling settings. Presets live in Library → Presets: "New preset", "Make one with your guide" (tell your guide how your stories should be told; see Making things with your guide), or "Import" a chat-completion preset JSON (Sola, Frankenstein and the like). Importing makes it the preset new stories begin with (Import says "Filed into presets · new stories use it now"); stories you already have keep theirs. Importing never changes where requests go: the file's connection settings (proxy, URL, models) are not read, and request fields it brings arrive switched off (see "Extra request fields"). A story uses one preset, chosen in Story Index → "Preset" ("Use" under "Attach"). Choosing another redraws the passages already on the page through its display regex. The built-in default can't be deleted, only put back ("Reset the default preset"); deleting another preset sends its stories to the default.

The preset sheet has four sections (on a phone, under "Sections"): "What it says" (the instructions, by what they do), "How it feels" (how bold, how long, how far it reads), "What it remembers" (its dials and variables, and where each is used) and "About this preset" (its name, how it is sent, its display scripts and own styles, export). It saves itself; "Save now" forces it.

"What it says": the preset's name, how many choices and blocks are on and about how many tokens they send before the story itself, "Add a dial", "Add a panel" and "Add a block" (on the list builder), and a bar of where those tokens go (the preset's core, its system blocks and your choices, or "its blocks, in order" for a preset without headings). Under it the blocks, as their author arranged them, whoever wrote the preset. Its heading blocks become its groups, in the order it sends them: a block that names a part rather than saying much itself, its name drawn as a rule ("━📁 Core", "━━━( Tone )━━━", "‒+ Tense", "---Tense---", "=Pick one POV 👇 =====", "### Style") or wholly in brackets ("【Extras】") when it sends nothing; a block named as a tag ("┌ <role>") is a wrapper, not a heading. Each group says how many of its blocks are on and what they cost; a preset without headings is one group, "Its blocks, in order". Some groups are one-of choices, and "Your choices" shows each as a dropdown ("One of each"; nine at first, then "Show all"): a group whose blocks each set the same variable (so only one can count), or each wrap their text in the same tag ("<tense>…</tense>") with at most one on; or one whose heading asks something ("━ How high are the stakes?"), says "pick one" or "enable only one" (itself, or from an empty heading above it, as Marinara's "Enable Only One Toggles" stands over its "‒+" questions), or whose blocks share a label ("[Core] POV: …"), when no more than one of its blocks was on as the sheet opened. A heading over blocks meant to be on together stays a group ("=Pick one Color Option" in Realistic Frankenstein, with three on), and "Choose as many as you want" never becomes a choice; what the sheet reads as a choice stays one until it is opened again, whatever is switched meanwhile. Choosing an answer switches that block on and the others under the question off, exactly as their own switches would ("None chosen" switches them all off; "Several are on" when more than one is); the pencil beside it opens the chosen answer; the question leaves out the heading's "pick one" and its notes in brackets, which stay on the heading's own block. Each row has its switch, its tokens, a line on what it is for (from the block's own {{// @tooltip …}} or comment, where it has one) and a grip (drag, or focus it and use ↑ / ↓; it moves within the order it is sent, across headings, never into a choice). "The story itself" gathers the blocks the app fills each turn: Character Description, Scenario, World Info, Chat History (the anchor, which cannot move to a depth) and the ✦ blocks, Aetheria's own: "Living pages", "The cast", "Story so far", "Story memory", "World", "Living receipt", "Response instructions" (with the author's note). Move them or switch them off like any block. When some ✦ blocks are not in the list, each is named with where it is sent anyway, and "Show Aetheria's blocks" puts them in the list to move or switch off; "Add the cast" adds the cast block. Blocks an imported preset's own order leaves out arrive switched off, marked "not in the imported order"; switch one on and it is sent where it sits, and an exported preset lists it there. Choosing a block opens it on the right, under "The block" (for one of a choice's answers, the eyebrow reads "A choice" and its question, "Chosen" stands in place of "On", and the other answers to its question are listed, to open): "On", "When it's sent" (on the list builder; see below), "Sent" ("In order", where it sits, or "In the chat", with "Depth" and "Order": depth 0 is after the newest message; at one depth a higher order goes later), "As" (System, User, Assistant), "Insert a dial…" (when the preset has dials: puts {{.name}} where the cursor is), "What it says" (its text and tokens; under it, which variables the block reads and sets, with a way to "What it remembers"), "Its name", where it is in the order with "Earlier" and "Later", "Duplicate" and "Delete". Dials are the settings a preset offers, in a "Dials" card at the top of "What it says" (shown once a preset has one): each with its control, its line and how many blocks read it, set to where it starts. A choice swaps whole blocks; a dial fills a value into the blocks that read it, written {{.name}} (or {{getvar::name}}). The pencil opens the dial under "The dial": "Shown as" (until a block reads the dial, its name follows), "Written in a block as" (renaming it renames it in every block that uses it), "Kind" ("Pick one" with "Its answers" and "Add an answer", "Switch", "Number" with "From", "To", "In steps of" and a "Unit" such as words, or "Text"), "Starts as", "Its line", "Each story can set its own" (on unless switched off), the blocks that read it, "Duplicate" and "Delete" (with Undo; blocks that waited for it are then sent every time). A dial's value goes into the request before the first block and holds for the whole of it: a block that sets the same name is not heeded. A switch reads as "on" or "off". Each story sets its own values in its Story Index, under the preset (see Story Index). "When it's sent", in a block (list builder): "With a dial", "Always" or "When a dial says so", then "Dial" and "Is" (a switch on or off, one of a pick-one's answers, text filled in or empty, a number at least or below a value, with "Than"); "Kinds of request" ("New replies", "New takes", "Continuing", "Write for me"; none chosen is every kind); and "Only for characters tagged" (any of the tags; the tags on your shelf are offered with how many cards carry each). The block's row says it ("only when "Show the HUD" is on · only for new takes"). Panels (list builder) are trackers the model keeps in its replies, such as a HUD of the day and place, how each person feels, or a bond meter, made without any regex. "Add a panel" adds one ("New panel", one field, "Where") and opens it under "The panel"; the "Panels" card in "What it says" lists each with its switch ("Send …"), its tag, fields, place, how it shows and what the model reads, and a pencil to open it. In a panel: "Its name"; "Its tag", what the model wraps it in (<hud> … </hud>; replies written before a change keep the old one); "Its fields, in the order the model writes them", each with its name, its kind ("A line", "A list", one item a line below its name, "A meter", a number from 0 to its top, up to 20, drawn as pips, or "A note", one line shown as a quote), "What the model writes there", "Earlier", "Later" and remove; "Add a field"; "Written" ("After the reply", the usual, or "Before it"); "On the page" ("Folded", one line of the fields chosen in "Its folded line shows", its first two when none are; "Open"; or "Hidden", where the model still keeps it); "The model reads it" ("Newest only", the usual, "Last 3" or "Every one": older panels leave what is sent, whole, while the page keeps them); "What the model is told", the instruction Aetheria writes from the fields and sends after the story (at the end of each reply add the panel, its lines in this order, a dash ("—") for anything that does not apply yet, carry on from the last panel and change only what this reply changed, never mention it in the story); "When it's sent", the same conditions as a block; "Duplicate" and "Delete" (with Undo). In the story the panel is a card by the passage in your Binding (see Chat); a value the model got wrong can be corrected there and is written into the passage, so the next reply reads it. Each story can show a panel its own way, from its Story Index. "What it remembers": every variable the preset uses, with how many and how many are worth a look; "Find a variable or a block…"; "Worth a look" (a name read but never set, which is always empty, or set but never read); "Dials"; "Kept by the blocks" (set as each reply is put together); "From the story" (what a story holds that the preset never names). Each row says where it is set and read, and, when a story told with this preset is open, what it holds there. Choosing one opens it under "The variable": its value in that story, "Set in" and "Read in" (each opens the block), and "Make it a dial" (a name set to several plain values across blocks becomes a pick-one of them, as Sola's mind would; one set to a single value becomes text starting there; the preset's text is not changed, the dial now rules the name) or "Change the dial". Exported as a chat-completion preset, a preset with dials carries them, a first block "✦ Dials (from Aetheria)" sets their starting values with {{setvar}}, and a dial condition is written as {{if}} around its block, so the file works in other chat apps at the preset's values; imported back, they are dials and conditions again. Kinds of request travel as the file's own injection trigger; a tag condition is kept in the file for Aetheria. "Add a block" adds a new one, switched on, just after the block you have chosen (or before the chat history when none is); added among a question's answers it is a new answer, switched off until you choose it.
Two builders

The list builder (imported chat-completion presets and every new preset) sends the blocks in list order with their roles, macros and depth injections, as chat-completion presets expect. The classic builder joins blocks into one system prompt and places Aetheria's context itself; "Move to the list builder" (at the head of "What it says", or "Use the list builder" in "About this preset") moves an older preset over, keeping its order. Switching "Use the list builder" off returns a preset to the classic builder.

"How it feels": "How bold" ("How far from the likeliest word it may wander": "Steady" 0.8, "Balanced" 1, "Adventurous" 1.15, or "Other"), and "Length and reach": "The longest a reply may run" ("Short" 1,000 tokens, "Medium" 4,000, "Long" 8,000, "No limit" 64,000, or "Other"; a ceiling, not a target) and "How much of the story it reads" ("32k", "128k", "All it holds", or "Other"; the whole request, the reply included). "Other" is chosen whenever the number is none of the steps. "The numbers" folds the exact settings, with what they are now: "Temperature", "Top P", "Frequency penalty", "Presence penalty", "Max response tokens" and "Context limit". The margin: "When in doubt" (Balanced), "Some models choose their own" (temperature and top P go to every provider except Claude models from 4.7 on, which refuse them (Haiku still takes them); Gemini 3 does best left at 1; the penalties go to OpenAI, OpenRouter, OpenAI-format proxies and local servers, not Anthropic or Gemini), and "On Ollama" (how much of the story it reads is also how much room Ollama gives the model).

"About this preset" (with "Add a script" at its head): "Its name"; "How it is sent": "Use the list builder", and on the list builder "Speaker names", "Merge consecutive system blocks", "Reasoning effort" and "Assistant prefill"; and, for any preset, "Extra request fields": fields added to a story reply's request as they are, for settings a provider takes that Aetheria has no switch for (Gemini's Flex tier as service_tier "flex", OpenRouter's provider order, a reasoning setting). Each has its name, its value in JSON ("flex", 0.5, true or an object; a bare word is taken as text), where it goes ("Every provider", OpenRouter, Google AI Studio, Google Vertex AI, Kimi, OpenAI, Anthropic, Custom proxy or "Local models") and its switch (Google Vertex AI reads Google's own format, so a field for every provider is not sent to it, only one meant for it, such as generationConfig or safetySettings); "Add a field"; "What a request to this provider carries" shows them for a provider you pick. Aetheria always sends the model, the messages, the prompt, the system text, the tools and streaming itself (for Vertex AI, its contents and systemInstruction): a field named for one of them is not sent, and says so. They go with story replies only, not with memory, chapter or world requests. Fields that come with a brought-in preset (a Lumiverse preset's custom body, a chat-completion preset's "include body") arrive switched off, saying where they came from, until you turn them on. "Display scripts": every regex script the preset carries, grouped by what it does ("Change how a reply looks", what you read while the story and the model keep the words; "Change what is sent", what the model reads, the page untouched; "Rewrite the message itself", as it arrives, kept that way) and then by the preset's own folders, each with how many of its scripts are on; "Find a script…" searches names and folders.
