items: "New chapter" follows the chapter you are in; from an earlier chapter it makes a second chapter with the next number, and the story forks there.
In a side scene the path has no "New chapter"; the composer's goes to the latest chapter.
On a phone only the open chapter's passages are loaded ("Opening the chapter…"); the other chapters' memory is recalled from disk when needed.

blocks.text: Deleting

A chapter's ⋯ menu on the Stories shelf has "Delete chapter" (its side scenes go too); "Delete story" (there, or at the foot of "The story" sheet) removes them all. There is no undo, and it stops at the first chapter that cannot be removed. A deleted chapter takes the sealed summary of the one before it with it; the story reads on from the latest earlier chapter.

pages.title: Side scenes and threads
pages.summary: Interludes and flashbacks played apart from the story, and threads: in-world time, the story clock, and sharing a passage into another story.

blocks.text: A side scene is an interlude or a flashback played apart from the story, from one passage: a passage's More, "Play a side scene from here…", or "Play a side scene…" (from the latest passage) in "The story" sheet and, on a phone, Story tools. The sheet asks "What kind" ("Interlude": beside the story at this point; "Flashback": from before this point, played now), "What it is about" (optional) and "Who is in it" (everyone unless you choose fewer); then "Begin the side scene".

It knows the story up to that passage and nothing after: what it is about, the passage, the sealed summaries before its chapter and, with story memory on, memory cut at that passage. It uses the story's model, preset, lorebooks and world; each reply is a normal request. Nothing in it reaches the story until it ends. It is not a chapter: no number, not on the chapter path, not exported. A banner sits above its passages ("A side scene from chapter 3: Interlude") with "Back to the story" (the scene stays as it is) and, while it is open:

items: "End and remember": one request to the memory model drafts what the story should remember; edit it, then "Keep it and end" (or "Write it again", "Not yet"). "Write it yourself" skips the request. It is kept as one remembered event at the passage the scene left from, and the scene becomes read-only.
"Clone": a new open scene with these passages so far (one take each), titled "…, retold". Inside a scene, a passage's More offers "Clone the scene from here".
"Make it a chapter" (it asks first): it joins the chapter path right after its chapter; later chapters move up one.
"Discard": no trace in memory; then "Play on" or "Delete" (which asks first).

blocks.text: An ended scene keeps "Clone", to play on from a copy. An ended or discarded scene has no composer; it is read, not written in. In the chapter, under the passage it left from, it is listed with "Return to it" or, once ended, "Read it". "The story" sheet lists them under "Side scenes"; the map hangs them beside their passage.
Threads
Neither of these sends a request.

items: Time: More → "Set when this happens…". "When" is in the story's own words ("Night, the third day"), shown over the passage where the time changes and carried on by memory. "On the story’s clock" (optional) is a day and a part of the day, which puts the story in order with itself and later beside another. "Set the time"; press the time over a passage to change it. Where a scene card heads the passage, the card's "When" shows the time instead, with "the story clock…" beside it.

Sharing: More → "Share into another story…". Neither it nor "Set when this happens…" is offered inside a side scene, and a shared copy cannot be shared on. Pick the story ("Into": it lands at the end of its latest chapter) and "Who learns it" (those in the scene there as memory has it, else the cast; untick any). "Share it" adds a copy marked "Shared · From …"; only those who learn it remember it later, and with no one it is only read. The original shows "Knot · Shared into …". Each mark has "Open" (that story's map at the passage) and "Unshare", which asks first ("Keep it" to leave it): the copy and what was learned from it go; the original stays. A shared passage chosen on the map lists it in the Inspector under "Knotted with", with "Open … at this passage" and "Unshare" (which does not ask). A shared copy cannot be edited or given new takes there, only where it began. The Inspector's Details lists the knotted stories under "Threads".

pages.title: The map
pages.summary: Every chapter and passage of a story, the takes you did not keep, the branches you carried on, notes, and beats planned ahead.

blocks.text: The map is a story's second view: the "Map" tab above the story, the map icon on the chapter path at its foot ("Open the map"), or "Map" in the chat's "Reading take …" note. It draws every chapter. Looking, choosing and switching takes here call no model.
Across the page (a desktop):

items: Your path, the passages the chat shows, is one lit line through every chapter: a dot per passage with its speaker and opening words. "✎ the story" at its start holds notes on the whole story, among them any the guide kept from "A look over this story" ("Keep to this: …", "A thread to bring back: …"), switched into the story's context.

Each chapter is headed by its roman numeral, its name (press it for the chapter's notes) and its own summary over a rule (sealed when the next chapter began; the newest chapter has none yet); across the page a faint line marks where it begins, and the chapter you are reading has its numeral and rule lit. Choosing a chapter on the chapter path brings it into view.

Over a passage: "where you are" (the end of your path in the open chapter), its takes count ("3 · 1 path"), "✎ 2" for notes, "✦ planned" if a planned beat was written into it, and a knot with the other story's name if the passage was shared into or from another story (see Side scenes and threads). Where a scene begins, a line under the passage says where, when and who is there ("◦" and the scene).

The takes count fans the takes out, favourites first: "●" is the one showing, "path" one the story carried on from. Pressing a card switches to that take, as the chat's take arrows do; its star marks a favourite.
A branch (another take carried on) drops into its own lane below and runs beside the line, fainter; its first passage says which take it grew from ("take 2 · Hesk").

Four or more passages in a row with nothing to mark fold into one segment ("12 passages", first and last lines, "N retried"); on a branch, two. Press to open; "fold 12 passages" folds it again. Forks, notes, plans still waiting, side scenes, passages shared with another story, the first passage, the end of your path and where you are never fold.

Planned beats are dashed cards after the line's end ("Planned") or beside their passage ("From here"). Side scenes hang as tipped-in cards ("Side scene" and how it stands): a double click or Enter opens one (even with nothing played in it yet); a click chooses it, and the Inspector says "Side scene" and its kind, its name and how it stands, what it is about, the passage it was played from, what its state means (an ended one shows what the story remembers of it), how many passages it has, "Return to it" (or "Read it" once ended or discarded) and "Show the passage it left from".

blocks.text: The bar on top gives the shape ("3 chapters · 48 passages · 9 takes, 2 paths"), a key and a hint (in windows wider than 1100 pixels), "Add a note" and "Plan a beat".
Choosing and reading

A click or Space chooses a passage: the Inspector shows it ("Passage") and "Read it in the chat ›" appears under it ("Read this branch ›" on a branch). A double click or Enter reads it at once: the Chat opens at that passage, in its chapter, and marks it for a moment. For a passage on another branch the Inspector first says which take reading it switches to, and its button reads "Read this branch in the chat"; your other path stays on the map, and the take arrows switch back. The Inspector also holds "The scene" (as memory read it, with "Correct the scene" where a scene begins or "A scene begins here" on a passage inside one, "Not a new scene", and "Open in the World" when worlds are on), "Notes on this passage" and "Planned from here".

Notes pin to the whole story ("Add a note"), a chapter or a passage. Each reads "Just for you" until its switch is on; then it is sent with every reply (a chapter's within that chapter, a passage's "from here on, while this passage is on your path") inside the story's usual request: no extra call, a few more tokens.
Planned beats

"Plan a beat" (or "Plan a beat from here" on a passage) asks for "The beat", in your words, and "When": "With the next reply", "When the scene reaches a place", "After a number of passages" or "When a preset flag is set" ({{setvar}}). Planning calls no model. A due beat goes out once, as a one-off instruction in the next reply's request to the story's model, to bring it about in its own way. One per reply, the first due in your order ("Earlier", "Later"); it then reads "Written", and every take of that reply is written from it. A beat planned from a passage waits while that passage is off your path; side scenes never take one. A chosen plan offers "Edit", "Set aside", "Plan it again", "Let it come anywhere" and "Remove".

Moving (desktop): drag from anywhere; the wheel moves along the line, Ctrl and the wheel (or a trackpad pinch) zooms. With the map focused: arrow keys pan, + and − zoom, 0 is actual size at where you are, Tab walks the passages. Bottom right: "−", the zoom percentage, "+", "Where I am". Far out, only the shape and chapter names show.

On a phone (or a map narrower than 600 pixels) it is one column that scrolls like a page; a branch is a line under its passage ("Branch from take 2 · 3 passages ▾") that opens in place. Two fingers pinch the column larger or smaller (it rewraps to fit, and the size is kept on this device; in a narrow window a trackpad pinch, or Ctrl and the wheel, does the same); "Where I am" scrolls the column to you, leaving "Add a note" and "Plan a beat" where they are. What you choose opens the Inspector as a sheet.

To try the map on a story with plenty of branches: Workshop → About, "Samples to try things out", "Show samples", then "Add a sample story with many branches" ("The Forking Road", which opens on the map). It is an ordinary story on your shelf, deleted the same way, and nothing is sent to a model.

pages.title: Story tools and the scene card
pages.summary: The tools a story can let its model use (dice, the scene, what people carry, travel, a picture), what each costs, and the scene card.

blocks.text: Story tools let the model change the story's state in the open: it asks, and the app does the work. They are all off unless you switch them on. Each story has its own switches, under "Tools the story can use" in the story's Details (on a desktop "The story" in the story's head; on a phone "Tools", then "The story"). Workshop → Reading has the same switches under "New stories": what a new story starts with. A tool switched on where it cannot work says why on its row ("Not used here: only for a story set in a world.").
The tools:

items: "Dice": the story can ask for a roll when chance should decide. The app rolls (seeded and kept), never the model, and shows it. Each roll adds a request to finish the reply.
"The scene": who arrives or leaves, and when the place or the time changes.
"What people carry": someone gains, loses, puts on or takes off something.
"Travel in the world": moves the party to a named place on the story's world map. Only for a story set in a world while "Worlds in stories" is on. Moving is free.

"A picture of the scene": asks your image source (Workshop → Image) for a picture, shown in the passage when it is ready. Each picture is a request to the image source, a paid one on NovelAI. It needs image generation set up.

blocks.text: A campaign has four more, in a closed "For the campaign" section: "Quests", "The party’s stores", "Skill checks" and "How people are" (see Campaigns).
What it costs

Each switch that is on sends its definition with every request (the Story Index counts them in a row of their own, "Story tools", and in its total). A call that comes mid-reply adds a request to the story's model to finish the reply, at most three requests a reply, all counted in that take's cost. With every switch off, nothing about tools is sent.
Two ways of asking

With Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter, a custom proxy and local servers in chat format, the model uses real tool calls. OpenRouter models that list no tool support (other than Claude) and every other provider, or text completion, get markers instead: the model writes something like ⟦roll 2d6+1: to force the door⟧ and the app takes it out of the passage and does the work. With a marker, the model is told to end its reply on the roll; the result shows at once, and the model reads it next turn. If a provider refuses tools for a model before writing anything, the reply is asked again once with markers, and the refusal costs nothing.

In the passage, each call is a quiet chip where it happened ("Rolled 2d6+1 → 9 · to force the door"), with a status when it is not simply done: "Working…", "Kept, not changed" (you had kept that field), "Failed" or "Undone". Open a chip to see "Asked", "Came back", the dice, and "How" (for a check, "The check" too). A change to the scene, what people carry, travel, a quest, the stores or a condition can be set aside with "Undo this change"; rolls and checks cannot. A tool's work belongs to its take: another take shows its own calls, or none.
The scene card

Where a scene begins, the manuscript shows a folded line: the place, the time and who is there. Opened, it shows "Where", "When", "Who", and what each person "Carries" and "Wears", each value tagged with where it came from (the memory pass, a tool, or you). Press a value to correct it; "Keep" stops later memory passes and tools from changing that field. A card carried over from the chapter before says so ("Carried on from the chapter before."). Beside "When", "the story clock…" sets a day and a part of the day (see Side scenes and threads). Notes under passages say what changed in the scene. It is read from story memory and the tools, and asks no model. Switch it with "Show the scene card" (on by default) in Workshop → Reading, or for one story in its Details; "Keep the scene's line in view" holds the current scene's line under the header (on by default on a desktop, off on a phone).

pages.title: Campaigns
pages.summary: A story run by a game master for a party in a world: quests, shared stores, checks the app rolls, and sessions with recaps.

blocks.text: A campaign is a story told by a game master to a party, in a world. Underneath it is an ordinary story (chat, map, chapters and memory work as usual) with a "Campaign" tab and a campaign block added to every reply.
Beginning one

On the Table press "Begin a campaign" (on a phone, "Campaign"). It is always there, and it always makes a new story ("A campaign in" and the world's name), leaving the bench alone. The sheet asks for:

items: "The world": required. Choose one, or "Make a world" (Library → Worlds). Your worlds are listed only while "Worlds in stories" is on (Library → Worlds): with it off the sheet may say "A campaign needs a world, and there is none yet." Turn it on and open the sheet again. When the worlds are listed but the switch is off, beginning switches it on.

"The party": your characters as chips, then "You play" ("No one in particular" to be yourself). The others are voiced by the game master until you let them speak from the cast. With no one chosen you play alone.

"The game master and the opening" (folded): "The game master (built in)", an ordinary editable card made once into your characters, or any character; and "Let the game master open" or "Open with a line" (their first words as you write them).

blocks.text: Then "Begin the campaign".
Set up by talking

In your guide's panel, "Make something" → "A campaign" (or ask them in words): a line or two about the campaign ("Smugglers in the sea caves of Lantern Quay. I play a customs officer new to the coast; Thorne dives with us"). One request sets it out on a card, from your shelf: "The world" (a world of yours when it fits, else "A new world, made now" with a line describing it), "The party" (the characters named or plainly suited, each with a switch, and "Add someone from the shelf…"), "You play" ("Someone of your own", or one of the party), and "The first quest" with what sets it going. Change any of it; "Begin the campaign" begins it as the sheet does (the game master, who opens when you ask, the party, the world and its tools), with the first quest already open in the journal. A new world is made first, its questions decided for them: three to five more requests and a few minutes. Then "Open the campaign".
An existing story

In its sheet ("The whole story" in the story's Details, or the story on the Stories shelf), under "A campaign", press "Run this story as a campaign…". Same form: its world (if it has one) comes chosen, its cast is the party (anyone added is voiced by the game master), whom you play stays, no opening. "Run it as a campaign" keeps every passage; the game master joins at the head of the cast, told every secret.
Tools

A campaign switches on "Dice", "The scene", "What people carry", "Travel in the world" and its own four: "Quests", "The party’s stores", "Skill checks", "How people are" (story tool switches, under "For the campaign"). Their definitions add tokens to every request. A call that comes mid-reply (always so for a roll or a check) adds a request to finish the reply: at most three requests a reply in all. Each call is a chip in the passage, where a change can be undone ("Undo this change"). For a check the app, never the model, rolls a d20 plus any modifier against a number or a word (very easy 5, easy 10, medium or moderate 15, hard 20, very hard 25, nearly impossible 30), with advantage or disadvantage when the game master calls for it, and tells the model whether it worked and by how much.

The campaign block, built with no call: that it is a campaign and who runs it (a party member the AI plays is told to play only them), the party, the world, the session, quests, the stores, how people are, what you keep, and the tools.
The Campaign tab ("The journal"; on a phone a sheet, "The campaign") reads as it stands on the path you are reading, so another take or branch shows it as it stood there:

items: "The party": each says "You play them", "Voiced by the game master" or "Speaks for themself", with conditions as chips you can clear.

"Quests": "Mark complete", "Mark failed", "Reopen", "Add a note" (each note links back to its passage, "at its passage"), "Keep" (tools leave it alone), "Take it off"; "Open a quest" (then "Open it"); "Finished".
"The party’s stores": − and +, "Keep", × to take it off, "Add to the stores" (a name and how many, then "Add"). In a campaign the scene card also shows "The party carries".
"Checks and rolls", the latest first: "at its passage" opens it on the map; older ones under "Earlier".
"Sessions": which session is being played, "End the session", the last recap, and "Earlier sessions" with theirs; between sessions, "Begin the next session".

blocks.text: The guide's tour

The first time a campaign's journal opens, your guide offers "A campaign": the party, quests, the stores, checks and rolls, sessions, and how the journal follows the path you read. Workshop → About has it too, for the open campaign.
Sessions

"End the session" is one request to the memory model (or the story's model, if memory uses it) for a recap you edit, then "Keep the recap" ("Write it again", "Not yet"); "Write the recap myself" skips it. A kept recap ends the session and joins the story's memory; the chat's head shows "Last time…" with "Begin the next session" (no request), "Open the journal" and, for a long recap, "Read it all". A campaign the game master opens starts with "The campaign is set": "Let the game master open" is one request to the story's model (your cue, "Begin.", goes on the page as your passage), or "I’ll write the first line".

pages.title: The Observer
pages.summary: The second reader beside the story: ask it about the story (or the app), and it answers without ever writing into the story.

blocks.text: The Observer is a second reader beside the story. It reads the story and answers questions about it, and never writes into it: nothing asked there is sent to the story. your guide is the default Observer. Its panel has two hats, "The story" and "The app": in "The story" it talks about what you are writing; in "The app" your guide answers questions about Aetheria itself, as the in-app guide.

Where it is. On a desktop, the composer's "Observer" button (it reads "Reading" while the Observer works) or Ctrl+O opens it as the "Observer" tab of the inspector on the right, beside "Details". Pressing the button again ("Put the Observer away") or closing the inspector puts it away. On a phone there is no composer button: open the story's "Tools" and press "Observer" (it says "Open lens", or "Watching" when open); it rises as a sheet with the tabs Details and Observer.
Asking

Type in its own small composer (Enter asks, Shift+Enter for a new line). Empty, it offers starter questions such as "Which threads are still left open?". "Ask again" on an answer re-asks the question and replaces that answer. Reasoning, if the model writes some, folds under "Reasoning". If the model sends back nothing (a busy free model, or one that spent its room thinking), it says so ("Error: The model sent back nothing. Ask again, or try another model."). A provider's error kept in the story is not read as a passage. "Clear" empties the conversation; the story is untouched. It is one conversation, the same whichever story is open, kept on this device (a phone keeps it too) until you clear it. It reads the open story's latest passages (up to twenty), numbered and marked with who speaks ("Reader" for yours), so it can point at the passage it means; your conversation with it; its prompt; and Observer recall when that is on.
Cost

Every question, starter or "Ask again" is one request, to the model chosen for the Observer: by default the model for everything else, which is the open story's own unless you chose another (a story's Models sheet → "Everything else", where "The Observer" can have its own; see Providers).

"Reads along on its own" (a switch at the panel's head and in Workshop → Observer; off by default) makes it take a look by itself every 5 replies, or as set by "Every how many replies" in Workshop → Observer. While it is on, the switch reads "Reads along: a look every 5 replies" (with your number). Only replies arriving while it is open count. Each look asks one of its six built-in questions about the story (such as "Which threads are still open, and which has waited longest?" or "Is the scene moving, or circling?"), which shows in the conversation like one of yours: one request. While it works, the line above the composer says "The Observer is reading", and the line under its own field says "Reading the story…".
Who it is. The sliders button at its head ("Who watches, and what it is told"):

items: "Who watches": "your guide (the guide)" or any character, who then reads the story in their own voice, still never writing into it.
"It knows you as": "No one in particular" or any character; separate from who you play.

"What it is told": its prompt. The built-in one is your guide's own: it tells them to stay out of the story and never roleplay; to answer what you asked first, briefly, pointing at the passage by its number or a few of its words; to know only what the passages show; to take the story on its own terms without moralising; to offer two or three ideas when asked, never writing your passage; and to be honest and specific about your writing. Maelis reads like a devoted reader (continuity slips, threads left hanging, a voice that changes, set-ups still waiting); Ilario like a lamplighter on his round (threads still burning or gone dark, doors nobody has opened yet, a scene that stalls, and continuity too). They guesses at what comes next only when asked, and says it is a guess; asked what could happen, Maelis reaches first for what is already planted, Ilario for a door not yet opened. Choosing the other guide in Workshop → About changes the built-in prompt with them; a prompt you wrote yourself stays yours. When a character watches, its own built-in prompt is used: the character talks about the story as themself, from outside the scene, briefly, pointing at the passage, about what people want, hide or avoid. "Save the prompt" applies yours from the next question; "Restore the built-in prompt" undoes it.

blocks.text: Workshop → Observer has the same: "Reads along on its own", "The Observer speaks as" (where your guide is listed as "The Observer"), "The Observer knows you as" and "System prompt". That field starts from the prompt the Observer is actually given: your guide's own, or the plain Observer's while a character watches. What you write there is kept when you leave the field, and "Restore the built-in prompt" (shown only for a prompt of your own) goes back.

Observer recall (Workshop → Memory) is its own memory of your conversations with it, searched by meaning; it never touches story memory. The phone app adds "Observer recall on this device", off by default because indexing is expensive on a phone.

pages.title: Providers and models
pages.summary: Keys for each provider, the models they offer, the default for new stories, a story's own model, local servers, your proxy, caching and cost.

blocks.text: Providers is the Workshop room for model access: keys, each provider's models, the default model for new stories, the model for everything else, local servers, your own proxy and prompt caching. Keys are kept in this device's secure storage, never in plain settings (on the desktop encrypted by the system where it can; on a phone in the app's private storage), and never shown again once saved.

The room opens on a plate saying where you stand: "Ready · one key" (or how many), "No OpenRouter key" (or whichever provider new stories use) when nothing could answer, "No key yet", "No model chosen", or "Ready · no key needed" (a local server or a proxy); then a sentence such as "New stories begin on Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B A55B (free), through OpenRouter. Everything else uses the story’s own model." Come from a story written on another model (the "Back to …" line at the top names it), and the plate adds that it keeps its own ("Juno keeps its own model: Gemini 3.8 Flash, through OpenRouter.") with "Use it for Juno too", which moves that story to the default, as its Models sheet would. The default is only for new stories; a story keeps its own model until you change it there or here. Below it: the card "Your keys", the card "Which model does what", and three folded lines, each with its state: "Saving money", "Your own endpoint" and "Local models". A margin lists "In this room" and has two notes, "Keys stay here" and "Spending less" (on a phone it comes last).
Keys

"Your keys" has a tile for each of OpenRouter, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google AI Studio and Google Vertex AI, marked "Connected" or "No key", and one for any other provider with a key. "Add a key" on a tile opens "API key for …" in it: paste the key and press "Save" ("Cancel" closes it); that provider's model list is fetched at once. A key added in the welcome starts you on a model from that provider's own list (with a Google key, Google's newest Flash; Gemini 2.5 and older no longer take new keys on AI Studio). A key added here changes no model: choose one from its "Models". "Add a provider", at the top of the room, opens a form for any provider without a key ("Add your first provider" when there are none): pick the "Provider", paste the "API key" and press "Save". Keys can be kept for OpenRouter, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google AI Studio, Google Vertex AI, Kimi, ElevenLabs and Hume AI (voices), NovelAI (pictures) and HuggingFace (only kept and tested). A connected tile says what happened last ("Saved securely on this device.", a test's answer) and has "Models" (chat providers only), "Test", "Replace" (a "New key for …" field) and "Remove" (with Undo). "Test" asks the provider whether it takes the key; it is free (Anthropic is asked for its model list). Google's two tiles test by counting the tokens of "Hi", which costs nothing, so a key that could only list models no longer passes.
Google's two ways in

Gemini is sold two ways, and each takes its own kind of key. "Google AI Studio" (its line: "Gemini, with an AI Studio key, and voices.") takes a key from aistudio.google.com; it also speaks the Gemini voices and offers "Gemini’s Flex tier". "Google Vertex AI" ("Gemini, with a Google Cloud key.") takes a key from Google Cloud: an express-mode key on its own, or a key from a Cloud project's credentials (bound to a service account) with that project. With the key field open, or once a key is kept, its tile shows "Project ID" (empty for an express-mode key) and "Region" ("global", or one such as us-central1); each is kept when you leave the field, and Test and every request use them. A Google Cloud key put under AI Studio lists AI Studio's models but cannot write there: AI Studio refuses it, and the error says to put it under Google Vertex AI. Vertex has no list of the models a key can use, so its "Models" gathers the Gemini models AI Studio (asked with the same key), OpenRouter and Aetheria know of, and asks Vertex to count a word with each, which costs nothing (it takes a few seconds). Models Vertex says it does not have are left out. One that would not count but that Vertex did not say it lacks (a new model may not count) stays, its row marked "not checked", and the list says "Vertex AI could not check the models marked “not checked”, so they may not answer." If Vertex could not be asked at all, every row is marked so. "Another model", above the list, takes any model id Vertex offers ("Use it"). Vertex reads Google's own format, which Aetheria writes for it: the preset's blocks before the story as one instruction, later ones as yours. Google keeps what repeats by itself there too.
Kimi

Kimi, from Moonshot AI ("Kimi K3 and K2, from Moonshot AI."), is added under "Add a provider" with a key from Kimi's platform (platform.kimi.ai). Its "Region" says where the key was made: "International" (api.moonshot.ai), or "China" (api.moonshot.cn) for a key from Kimi's China platform; the add form and Kimi's tile both have it, and "Test" asks Kimi's model list there (free), saying which region to try when the key is refused. Its "Models" lists what Kimi offers (Kimi K3, K2.6, K2.7 Code). Kimi's list can be days late with a new model (Kimi K3.1 Pro, kimi-k3.1-pro, when it came out), so "Another model", above the list, takes any model id Kimi offers ("Use it"), as Vertex's does. Kimi's models fix their own sampling, so a preset's temperature, top P and penalties are not sent to it. They think before they answer, shown folded like other models' thinking, and the thinking gets 32,768 tokens of room beyond the preset's reply length, so a reply is not cut off mid-thought. Kimi K3 takes the preset's "Reasoning effort" (Minimal and Low as low, Medium and High as high; Auto leaves Kimi's own, the most thorough, which is slower and costs more). Kimi keeps what repeats by itself, and its replies count what it read back.
The default model

"Which model does what" leads with "New stories begin on": the default, the models you chose lately, and "From a provider’s models…", which opens that provider's list. "Models" on a tile opens the same list under the tiles ("OpenRouter’s models", with "Fold it away"): "Search models", "Refresh", and on OpenRouter "Best value" (capability per cost). Models you chose lately collect under "Recently used" at the top (up to five). A model put in by hand under "Another model" (Vertex and Kimi) stays in that provider's list from then on, marked "added by you" with an × to remove it, until the provider lists it itself. Rows show the name, the id and, when known, how many tokens it reads; the default is marked "Current". Choosing one makes it the default for new stories, as the plate then says. your guide answers on this default too (unless you choose another under "Everything else"); the Observer answers on the open story's own model. Listing models costs nothing.
A story's model

On the desktop press the model chip in the story's head ("Choose a model" when none is set); on a phone, "Tools", then "Change model". The Models sheet lists OpenRouter, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google AI Studio, Google Vertex AI, Kimi, Custom proxy, Ollama, LM Studio, KoboldCpp, llama.cpp and Custom models, with the chosen provider's models beside; on a phone, "Provider" above the list chooses whose models it shows (and "Everything else"). OpenRouter's Google models ("Google: Gemini …") are OpenRouter's, sent with your OpenRouter key; Google AI Studio's are sent with your AI Studio key, and Google Vertex AI's with your Google Cloud key. A reply that failed names the provider it failed on, whichever the story is on now. Choosing sets the model for the whole story, every chapter of it (a side scene keeps its own); other stories keep theirs. Choosing here also becomes the default for new stories (the sheet says so: "new stories begin on the one you chose last"). A failed reply's "Choose a model" opens the same sheet.
Models for everything else

The story is written on its own model; everything else the app asks a model for can use another. In a story's Models sheet, "Everything else" (under "Besides the story" in its list), and in Workshop → Providers under "Which model does what", the same choices: "Everything else" itself ("The story's own model" by default, a model used lately, or "Another model…", a provider and the model's name, then "Use it"), and folded under "Choose for each" (which says how many are "chosen apart", and names them), one for each kind, each "Same as everything else" unless you choose: "Remembering" (the memory pass, closing a chapter, the stewards, side-scene and campaign summaries; the same choice as Library → Memory's), "The Observer", "The guide's answers", "Making things" (what the guides make, and ideas from what you enjoy; the same choice as "Made with" in your guide's panel) and "Worlds" (building a world from its book or a lorebook, and noticing what the story changes in it). Each row says which model it uses now. A cheaper model for everything else saves money without touching the story's own. The Studio keeps its own choice on its page, and a chapter's summary its own in "New chapter", in the model list beside "Write it for me" (the current provider's models).
Custom models
"Custom models" (under "Your own endpoint", and in the sheet) adds a model by hand: "Model id" exactly as the endpoint expects it, "Display name", "Add model". They are sent through the custom proxy.

Local models, folded under "Local models" (its line says "On this computer, free", or which server new stories use). "Look for local models" asks the usual ports (Ollama 11434, LM Studio 1234, KoboldCpp 5001, llama.cpp 8080) and any saved address, and says what answered. If a server answers at its usual address rather than the one saved, its row offers "Use that address". Each server has "Models" and "Settings": "Address"; "Format", either "Chat" (the server wraps each message for its model) or "Text completion" (the story written as one prompt in an instruct template); with "Text completion", "Template" ("Auto (from the model’s name)", ChatML, Llama 3, Mistral [INST], Alpaca, Vicuna, Gemma, Phi-3, Command-R); and for KoboldCpp and llama.cpp "Key, if the server asks for one". A model with no chat template of its own is flagged: "This model carries no chat template; Text completion suits it better." Local replies cost nothing. On a phone, "localhost" is the phone: give each server the computer's address on your network (like http://192.168.1.20:11434) and let the server listen beyond the computer; the Android app may use plain http there.

Custom proxy, folded under "Your own endpoint" (its line says "Not set", or the address and format). "Base URL" (an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, usually ending in /v1), "Request format" ("OpenAI" or "Anthropic"), "Skip SSL verification" (only for a local endpoint you control) and "The proxy’s models". This room has no key field for the proxy; the welcome (Workshop, About, "Show the welcome again") takes one as "Proxy key (only if it asks for one)".

Prompt caching, folded under "Saving money" (its line says "On for Claude and Qwen", or "Off", and "Gemini Flex" when that is on). Memory, the world and lorebook entries that fired on their keys sit inside the story, two passages from the end, so the start of each request repeats; OpenAI, Gemini, DeepSeek, GLM and most others reuse it by themselves, through your own endpoint in OpenAI's format too. Claude and Qwen are told what to keep: "Claude through Anthropic" and "Claude and Qwen through OpenRouter" are on by default (Qwen keeps five minutes either way; Gemini on OpenRouter is not marked, because it reads only the last mark, which moves every reply); on OpenRouter each story also asks to stay with one provider for ten minutes, so what any model keeps is still there for the next reply; "Claude through the custom proxy" is off and needs the Anthropic request format. "Keep it for": "Five minutes" or "An hour". Keeping costs a quarter more than sending, once; reading back costs a tenth; an hour costs twice as much to keep. It makes no extra calls. "Gemini’s Flex tier", below it: "Off" (the usual), "Remembering and worlds" or "Everything". Flex is Google's half-price tier for Gemini through your own AI Studio key (not through OpenRouter or Vertex AI); what is read back from Gemini's cache costs less too. A Flex request can take minutes rather than seconds, so "Remembering and worlds" (the memory pass, closing a chapter, the stewards, summaries, building a world and noticing its changes) suits it best: they run while you read. When Google is too busy for Flex, Aetheria asks again at the normal price, so nothing fails for it. Google's free tier does not offer Flex. A line below reports the last reply's tokens sent and read back from the cache (Gemini's too), and says when a reply came at the Flex price.
Cost

The desktop story head shows an estimate for the next reply; press it for the breakdown. It prices the request as it will be sent (story tools included), a reply as long as the story's last few were (1,000 tokens before it has any, never more than the reply's allowance), and as much of the request read back from the cache as the last replies on the same model had ("Of them, from the cache"), at the model's own cache price where OpenRouter lists one. In the Story Index, "What this story has cost" opens the ledger: an estimated price, requests, tokens sent, from the cache and written, by chapter and by day. It counts every take's requests and the story's other requests (memory passes, closing a chapter, summaries, the stewards, the world noticing its changes, the Observer), split by what they were for, priced at published rates (local ones at zero). Under "Saving money", below the last reply's line, one more line adds up what was asked outside any story on this device (the last 300 requests): "the guide’s answers" and "making" (characters, presets, worlds and the rest made with a guide or in the Studio), each with its requests and an estimated price.
Errors

A reply that fails reads "The page tore before the reply was written." with a plain reason (no key yet, the key refused (a Google Cloud key under AI Studio, or a Vertex key that needs its project), the provider not serving that model here (some free models only answer certain apps), out of credit, asked to slow down, the story too long for the model, a local server not answering at its address, the model declining to write it, the provider having trouble) and "Try again", "Open Providers" or "Choose a model". "What the provider said" folds out the provider's own words.

pages.title: Appearance: Bindings and comfort
pages.summary: Bindings (the themes), your own colours, motion and effects, and the size of the interface and the prose.

blocks.text: Workshop → Appearance changes how the house looks. Nothing here touches your stories.
Bindings
A Binding is a theme. The house Bindings each have their own ornament, corners and frames, not only colours:

items: Gilt & Slate, the default: frosted glass on slate, framed in gilt, set in Garamond.
Moonlit Silver: moons and stars.
Verdigris & Brass: leafy brass filigree.
Blossom & Rose Gold (light) and Plum & Blossom (dark): the sakura.

blocks.text: Press a card to wear it ("Wear this"; the one you wear says "Worn now"). Under "Other Bindings", "More Bindings" opens recolours of the same house: the glass, frames and type stay, only the colours change. Press one to wear it; while you wear one, that grid stays open.

Every Binding draws its controls with its own mark: the four-pointed star (Gilt & Slate, and every Binding that is not a house one, in its own colour), the blossom (the two sakura), the crescent (Moonlit Silver) or the leaf (Verdigris & Brass). A button is a plate of glass with its corners cut and the mark in the cuts: an everyday button has a mark at two corners, the one main action on a screen is filled with the Binding's colour and has a mark at all four, and a button that deletes something has red lines and no marks. A switch is a pointed jewel whose handle is the mark: dim at the left when off, lit at the right when on. A slider is a line marked in tenths, lit up to its value, with the mark for a handle. A choice of a few is a row of words with marks between them, the chosen one underlined as a tab is. A one-line field is a ruled line that lights while you type; a long one has a line down its left edge, as a passage does. Sheets, menus and dialogs are square, with the mark inside each corner. The composer is a plate of glass with its corners cut and one fine line round it, and Send is its arrow alone. A card has a frame inside its edge with the mark at its head and its foot, and keeps its rounded corners.

Light or dark: there is no switch that follows your computer. For a light house, wear Blossom & Rose Gold; among the Other Bindings, Vellum, Kintsugi, Paper & Ink, Sakura Light and Frosted Dawn are light. The rest are dark: Midnight Ink (the former house look), Cosmos, Grimoire, Noir, Deep Ocean, Wet Obsidian, Velvet Candle, Shadow Magic and Cyberpunk.
Every Binding colours a passage three ways

The text is in its own colour; speech (in quotation marks) is in the Binding's voice colour, the rose a speaker's name is set in; an aside (in italics: a thought, an action) is quieter, in whichever of the Binding's other colours stands furthest from both. Each is made light or dark enough to read on the Binding's glass. A Binding of your own gets them too. Lists of choices (a "Page" or an "Engine") open as a menu in the same glass and gilt, on a phone as on a computer, and a long text field grows with what is written in it.

"Bind your own" makes a Binding of your own: a "Name" and fifteen colour tokens, seeded from the Binding you wear (or your own, if you made one; one your guide designed keeps its ornament while you change its colours). Each change is worn and kept as you make it, in place of whatever you wore (a house Binding too): a colour shows as you drag it and is kept once you let go. It is a card under "More Bindings", and "Edit your Binding" changes it later. "Done" closes the editor; "Put back" returns to what you wore when you opened it, and your own Binding as it was. Only the material is yours: the layout, density and navigation stay as they are.
A Binding designed with your guide

In their panel, "Make something" → "A Binding": a line or two about the look ("Deep teal glass over black lacquer, copper hairlines, warm cream type"). One request: the model chooses dark or light, the fifteen colours (told what each is for: the grounds, the gilt, the text, your own light, memory's colour, a voice's colour, the signals), the light it gives off, and which of the house's ornament sets it draws (stars and an astrolabe, moons and constellations, vines and leaves, or blossom). Then every colour is read against the glass it sits on and made lighter or darker, keeping its hue, until it can be read; a ground too light for a dark Binding (or too dark for a light one) is moved the other way; a signal that does not look like its meaning takes the house's. The card shows the Binding's specimen, its name and note, and what was made easier to read. "Wear it" keeps it as your own Binding (replacing one you made before) and wears it at once, in place of the house colours; then "Change its colours" opens Appearance (where "Edit your Binding" has it) and "Back to the house" wears the house Binding you had before. "Design another" asks again; "Leave" keeps nothing.
The command bar lists every Binding by name ("Wear · " and its note); choosing one wears it at once, as its card here does.
Motion and effects:

items: "Motion scale": scales the house's transitions, from 0 to 150% (100% to begin with); at zero, nothing animates at all, the falling petals included.

"Ambient atmosphere" and "Effect level" (0 to 3, starting at 1) are kept, but in this version nothing behind the interface reads them, so neither changes what you see (at 3, a phone shows streamed text in slightly larger steps).

blocks.text: On a slower machine, Workshop → Archive's "Quality profile" also reduces motion and effects: "Full" (where a computer begins), "Balanced" (where a phone begins: motion at most 100%, 90% on a phone or a narrow window, effects lowered, softer blur) or "Efficient" (motion at most 75%, no effects, no blur behind the panes, the petals at rest).
Scale:

items: "Interface scale" (desktop): everything in the window, larger or smaller, 80% to 140%.
"Manuscript text": the size of the story's prose and of what you write, 80% to 160%.

blocks.text: How wide the story's column is lives in Workshop → Reading ("Reading width"), not here.

pages.title: Reading: what the page shows
pages.summary: How wide the story reads, reasoning, timestamps, lore links, branching, the scene card, tidying older passages, and quick commands.

blocks.text: Workshop → Reading holds how the manuscript reads, and a few defaults for new stories.
What the page shows:

items: "Reading width" (desktop): "Comfortable" keeps shorter lines with margins on a wide window; "Wide" (the default) grows with the window up to lines you can still follow; "Full" uses the whole pane. It covers the passages, the composer and the scene line. A phone has no such setting: there the story always takes the full width of the screen, with narrow margins and a smaller portrait beside each passage.

"Show reasoning by default": a model's thinking opens without a click. With a preset of the app's older kind (not the house preset or an imported one that keeps its own order) it also adds a line to each request asking the model to put its reasoning in think tags.
"Message timestamps" (on by default): the time beside each passage's actions.

blocks.text: Type and colour, with a line of a passage shown as it will read:

items: "Narration": the face the story is set in: "EB Garamond (the house’s)", "Crimson Text", "Merriweather", "Roboto Slab", "Inter (sans-serif)", "Open Sans (sans-serif)" or "This device’s own (sans-serif)". All are carried by the app, on a phone too; each is sized to read like the house's.
"Speech": "As the narration" (the usual) or a face of its own from the same list, sized to sit level with the narration.
"Speech in italics" (on by default): off, speech is upright and told apart by its colour alone.
"Speech colour" and "Italics colour": off, each is the Binding's own; on, choose your own, kept in every Binding.
"Lore links in the manuscript": words that woke a lorebook entry are underlined.

"Swipe branching" (on by default): any reply can get new takes, and writing on from an older take forks the story, which is what the map reads. Switch it off and only the latest reply can be given new takes; its takes stay under its arrows, nothing forks, and an edit has no "Save as a new path".

"Show the scene card" (on by default): where a scene begins, a line with the place, the time and who is there, opening to what each carries and wears, as memory and the story's tools have it on the take you are reading. It shows only once a story has a scene, and a story can choose otherwise in its Details. "Keep the scene's line in view" pins it under the header while you read the current scene; it starts on for a desktop and off on a phone.

blocks.text: What the model reads:

items: "Tidy older passages" (on by default): past the latest few, a passage is sent without its folded sections, trackers and markup, only its words. A tracker the model writes in a tag of its own in most replies, on lines of its own with labelled fields (<status>Health: 80 · Mood: wary</status>), goes whole, text and all; a tag around the prose itself (a line of speech, a narrator's aside) keeps its words. It saves tokens on presets that write status panels. Presets that tidy their own (Savers, like Sola's) are left to them, except for a tracker their Savers do not name, such as one an earlier preset of the story left in its older replies; what is kept on the page is never changed. "Latest passages sent whole" (4 at first, up to 40) sets how many stay complete; a few more may go whole at times, so a provider can reuse the start of the story from its cache.

blocks.text: New stories:

items: "Tools the story can use": the story tools a new story starts with. Each story keeps its own switches in its Details (see the story tools page).

Quick commands: which commands the star (✦) beside the composer offers: "New chapter", "Generate an image", "Attach an image", "Voice mode", "Guide this reply", "Play as…", "Write as you" and "Response instructions". Switching one off takes it out of that menu. Commands added by plugins always show there and are not listed here.

blocks.text: The "Worlds in stories" switch is not here; it lives with the worlds, in Library → Worlds. The reply chime ("Message sound") is in Workshop → Voice, and the size of the story's text ("Manuscript text") in Workshop → Appearance.

pages.title: Voice: reading aloud and voice mode
pages.summary: Reading passages aloud, each character’s voice, voice mode for speaking to the story, and the reply chime.

blocks.text: Workshop → Voice is how stories are read aloud and how you can speak to them.
Speech out ("Text to speech"):

items: "Engine": "This computer's voice" (no setup, the default), "Kokoro (local Python, needs setup)" on a desktop, or a voice service: OpenAI, Google Gemini, ElevenLabs or Hume AI. A service needs its key (Workshop → Providers; Google Gemini's voices use the Google AI Studio key) and is billed by that service per use. If you already have a key for one, the room offers to use its voices.
Kokoro runs on your computer in Python and needs its packages and voice model installed beside the app; without them, Speak says it cannot start.
"The narrator's voice": reads the narration, and anyone without a voice of their own. A character's own voice is set on their card, under Voice, and travels with the card's PNG or CHARX file.

Choosing a voice: "Hear it" plays a short sample (a service bills it like any reading). ElevenLabs lists the voices on your account with "List my voices", or takes a voice id typed in. Hume AI is given a sentence describing the voice rather than a voice to pick.
"Speed", "Volume", and "Message sound" (a soft chime when a reply finishes).

blocks.text: Speaking a passage
Each passage has a Speak button among its actions ("Stop speaking" while it reads). If a voice fails, the message says why and offers "Use the system voice" or "Open Voice".
What is read aloud:

items: "Read aloud as": "The whole passage, in one voice" (the default); "Narration and speech, each in its own voice"; or "Only what people say". A quoted line goes to the character named beside it ("said Wren", "Kazriel:") or named at the start of the sentence just before it on the same line; otherwise to whoever last spoke on that line, else to whoever wrote the passage. A long passage is read only to about its first 3,000 characters. Nothing is sent to a model to decide.

"Skip actions in asterisks" (off by default), "Skip trackers and folded sections" (on by default), and "Read your passages in your character's voice" (off by default; gives your own passages a Speak button too).

blocks.text: Speech in ("Voice mode"): you speak, it writes and sends, and the reply is read back before it listens again ("Read replies aloud"). Voice mode is in the desktop app only; a phone does not offer it. Turn it on from the composer's star menu ("Turn voice mode on"), or with Ctrl+M (Cmd+M on a Mac). The "Recognition engine" is Local Whisper, which runs on this computer and needs its model in the app folder; without it, voice mode says so. "Auto-send delay" is the silence before a phrase is sent, and "Silence sensitivity" sets what counts as silence.

pages.title: Image: pictures for stories
pages.summary: Where pictures come from (ComfyUI on your computer, or NovelAI), making one in a story, and what the image workspace can and cannot do.

blocks.text: Workshop → Image sets up where pictures come from. Making them happens in a story, from the composer.
"Default source": the "Provider" is "ComfyUI (local)", a ComfyUI server you run yourself, or "NovelAI", a hosted service billed by NovelAI with its key in Workshop → Providers.

items: "Negative prompt": what "Leave out" starts with each time you make a picture; change it there for one picture.
"Quality suffix": the words the "Prompt" box starts with. With NovelAI they are also added at the end of what is sent.

ComfyUI: "Server URL" (for example http://localhost:8188) and its "Model", which must be the name of a checkpoint your ComfyUI has. It starts as "model_name", and until it is changed every ComfyUI picture stops and asks you to name one of your checkpoints as the "Model" here.

NovelAI: its "Model". Each NovelAI picture made with "Generate an image" first has NovelAI's own text model sum up the character card (for a scene, its scenario) into a description, so it is two requests to NovelAI. A picture the story asks for itself (the story tool) is one request, at a 16:9 shape.

blocks.text: Making pictures in a story:

items: The composer's star menu (✦) has "Generate an image" and "Attach an image". Either can be switched off in Workshop → Reading, under Quick commands.

"Generate an image" asks "What to draw" ("Character portrait" or "Scene illustration"), a "Prompt", what to "Leave out", the "Shape" ("Square (1:1)", "Portrait (3:4)", "Landscape (4:3)", "Landscape (16:9)" or "Vertical (9:16)") and the "Generator" ("ComfyUI" or "NovelAI Diffusion"; "For this image only; your default is unchanged."), then "Generate". The picture arrives as a passage in the story and is kept there.

With ComfyUI, what is sent is the "Prompt" box as you leave it: the automatic description of the character or scene is used only when the box is empty. To draw someone, describe them in "Prompt", or empty it. With NovelAI the card's summary comes first, then your prompt, then the suffix.
A "Character portrait" made here is a picture in the story. It does not change the card's portrait: set that in the character's sheet, under "Portrait & motion".

The story tool "A picture of the scene" lets the story's model ask for a picture as it writes. It is off unless you switch it on (see the story tools page), it waits until this room is set up (for ComfyUI a "Server URL", for NovelAI a key), and each picture is a request to your image source: paid on NovelAI, free on your own ComfyUI.

blocks.text: The image workspace
"Open image workspace" opens "Image Generator", a separate workspace with "Generate", "Upload" and "Library". What it does and does not do:

items: It makes pictures with ComfyUI; NovelAI is not offered there. It has its own prompt, size, steps and sampler fields, and uses this room's ComfyUI "Server URL" and "Model" (unless you give it a server of its own); this room's "Negative prompt" is not used there.

Its "Library" keeps only pictures made in the workspace, and only the latest (about 3 MB of them; the oldest go first). Pictures made in a story stay in that story. "Upload" only shows a picture; it is not kept.

The × at its top right ("Back to the Image room") takes you back to Workshop → Image. Opened from the Workshop it has no "Use Image": there is nothing there to use a picture for, so keep one with "Download" or "Copy URL".

blocks.text: Nothing here costs anything until a picture is asked for.

pages.title: Plugins: extensions
pages.summary: Installing extensions, what each may do, switching them on, safe mode, and taking them off.

blocks.text: Workshop → Plugins is the plugin registry: extensions that add commands, passage actions or settings of their own, and with the right permission read or write stories, change what the model is sent ("prompt.hooks") or restyle the app ("styles.inject").
Installing:

items: "Install from URL": a direct link to an .aetheria-plugin.zip package, then "Install URL".
"Install package": choose a package file from this device.

blocks.text: A package is a .aetheria-plugin.zip (a manifest and its code, at most 25 MB); extensions made for other chat apps are not packaged this way and do not install. Import does not install plugins: it takes any .zip for an archive backup and offers "Open the Archive". Install plugins here.
A new plugin is installed switched off. Its card shows the permissions it declares, as chips, so you can read what it asks for; "Enable" switches it on. Install only packages you trust.
Each installed plugin shows its name, version, author and where it came from (local or url), its description, a state ("Active", "Ready", "Off" or "Loading"), any error it reported, and:

items: "Enable" / "Enabled", to switch it on or off;
"Settings · N", when it has settings panels of its own ("Close settings" folds them);
"Uninstall", which asks first ("Uninstall this plugin?"): the package and its files are removed, and your stories and archive objects are not changed.

blocks.text: Safety:

items: "Plugin safe mode": installed plugins stay dormant; nothing of theirs runs until you turn it off, and a plugin's "Enable" or "Enabled" cannot be pressed while it is on ("Disable every plugin" still works).
"Disable every plugin" switches them all off at once.
If the app's last session ended badly, the next start keeps plugins from activating, and the room says so.

blocks.text: "Refresh" reads the registry again.

pages.title: Archive and About: backups, updates and the guide
pages.summary: Backups and restoring, finding lost conversations, diagnostics, performance, updates, the welcome, sample stories, and the guide’s tours.

blocks.text: Workshop → Archive keeps your work safe. Stories and settings are written to disk as you go; a backup is a portable copy you can move between machines.

items: "Export conversations": every story, as a backup file. It is saved straight to your Downloads folder (aetheria-conversations- and the time, .zip), without asking where.
"Export everything": the whole archive, with characters, lorebooks, presets, worlds, memories, settings and the Observer's conversation. It asks where to save the file.
"Scan for lost conversations" (Android app only): rebuilds stories whose files are on the phone but have gone missing from the list. On a desktop it ends with "Recovery scan: It did not finish."

"Import from Aetheria" appears when an older Aetheria archive is found: "Review discovered archive", then "Copy and restart" (close the older Aetheria first). Its whole data folder is copied, the older archive is never changed, and this archive is kept as a copy to return to. In the Android app the section is always there, with "Locate legacy ZIP" (or "Choose a different archive") and "Search again"; the archive is checked before "Import archive" replaces anything.

"Quality profile": "Full" (where a computer begins), "Balanced" (where a phone begins) or "Efficient". Lower profiles reduce motion and effects on slower machines; Efficient also drops the blur behind the panes (see Appearance). An older archive's Battery Saver or Ultra Safe shows as its own choice.
"Export diagnostics": a plain-text report of compatibility and recent logs, to read before you share it.

"Restore everything" replaces the whole archive (stories, characters, lorebooks, presets, worlds, memories and settings) with a backup file ("Choose a file"). An "Export everything" file restores only on the same kind of app (desktop to desktop, Android to Android); to move stories between a phone and a computer, use "Export conversations" and "Restore conversations only". "Restore conversations only" adds the stories from a conversations backup beside the ones you have; a story that is already here comes in as a copy. After either, the line beneath says what came back, and to restart Aetheria to see it.

blocks.text: If the app hits an error it shows "Oops! Something went wrong", with "Error details (click to expand)" and "Reload Page". Your stories are already on disk. If it happens again, "Export diagnostics" makes a report you can read before sharing.
Workshop → About:

items: The version and runtime; "Check for updates", then "Download update" and "Restart and install" when there is one.

"Show the welcome again": the first-evening welcome (your name, the look, a model and a character). When it closes, finished or skipped, the guide offers their tour of the house, with "Skip the tour", but only if that offer was never answered; "Offer every tour again" brings it back. The tour goes on into setting out the starter set on the table, which is offered on its own if the tour is skipped.

The guide: who guides you (the two guides, by their portraits; see The guide); "Show me around" (the house), "A story’s page", "The map", "The world", "A campaign", "Your first story" (while some of the starter set is in the archive), and "Ask your guide". "Offer a tour the first time I open something" turns their offers on or off, and "Offer every tour again" makes each one new. Tours make no model call; questions use your own model.
"What your guide thinks you enjoy" (see its page).
"The starter set": Lantern Quay, which comes with a new archive (see its page). "Bring in Lantern Quay", "Put back what is missing" and "Set the table with your guide".
"Samples to try things out": "Show samples", then "Add a sample story with many branches" (The Forking Road, for exploring the map; it opens on the map, and adding it again makes another copy).

blocks.text: The guide is also under ? in the rail (on a phone, under More), and in the Observer panel's "The app" hat. Their panel, their tours and what a question costs are on their own page (The guide).

pages.title: your guide, the guide
pages.summary: your guide themself: where their panel is, asking them, "Show me", what a question sends and costs, what they keeps, and their tours.

figures.alt: The choice of guide: Maelis or Ilario

blocks.text: your guide is the in-app guide. They answers questions about how Aetheria works, gives scripted tours, and points at things on the screen. They is also the default Observer (see that page): there they reads your story; here they talks about the app.
Two guides

Two gods keep the house, and you choose which shows you round: Maelis, Keeper of the Last Page, a goddess of knowledge (quick, curious, a little nosy; she knows everything that has happened and nothing that hasn't), or Ilario, Lamplighter of the Unwritten, a god of beginnings (steady, warm, gently teasing; he keeps a lamp lit in every story not yet finished and knows none of their endings). They know the same things, give the same tours and point at the same places; each says it in their own way, and each reads your story differently as the Observer. Neither knows what happens next in your story. The first time the welcome closes, "Who shows you round?" offers both (or "Skip the tour" keeps Maelis); choose again any time in Workshop → About, under "The guide", where both guides' portraits are. Your conversation with the guide carries on whichever you choose.

New in 1.5. An archive from before 1.5 is told what is new once, on the Table, in a card headed "Since you were last here": "A second guide" (choose Maelis or Ilario there), and "Lantern Quay", whose button ("Bring them in and set the table", or "Set the table with them" if the set is already in) brings in the starter set if it is missing and starts "Your first story". "Not now" closes the card for good and the setting-out is not offered again; it stays in Workshop → About. A new archive is not shown the card: it meets both on its first evening.

Where they is. On a desktop, "?" in the rail (tooltip "your guide, the guide"); on a phone, "More", then "your guide". Also the command bar's "Ask your guide", "Ask your guide" in Workshop → About, and the Observer panel's "The app" hat. It is one conversation wherever you open it. Their panel lists their tours as buttons ("Show me around", "A story’s page", "The map", "The world", "A campaign", and "Your first story" while some of the starter set is in the archive); in the Observer's hat the panel is shorter and has no tour buttons. Once there is a conversation (or "Make something" is open), the head folds to a small picture and their title, with "Tours" to unfold the tour buttons ("Hide the tours" folds them again), so the conversation has the room.
Asking

Type in "Ask your guide about the app…" and press Enter (Shift+Enter for a new line), or the arrow ("Ask"). With nothing asked yet, the panel offers four starter questions, such as "What does the Story Index show?". While they thinks their answer reads "Thinking…"; "Stop" ends it, keeping what they had said so far. When pointing would help, their answer carries a "Show me:" button naming the place (three at most). Pressing it closes the panel, goes there first (a story's map, a world's room) and points, with "Got it" to finish; a place inside a story needs one open ("Open a story first, then I can show you that right where it is."). "Clear", at the foot once you have asked something, empties the conversation at once. If the provider refuses, their answer says why in plain words.

What a question sends, and what it costs. Each question is a request to your own model: the one chosen for "The guide's answers", which by default is the model for everything else: the default from Workshop → Providers (the one last chosen for a story), unless you chose another under "Everything else" (see Providers). The foot of their panel names the model and about how many tokens a question sends ("Asks … · about 9.4k tokens a question"). With no model set up it says "Questions use your own model, and none is set up yet.", the field reads "Choose a model in Workshop → Providers first", and nothing can be asked. A question sends their own instructions, the places they can point at, the overview page and the list of their pages, a few pages (the one for the screen you are on and those your question matches best), a few lines about where you are (the screen, phone or desktop, your provider and model, how many stories and characters you have, and for an open story its name, chapters, model, whether it has a world or is a campaign, and which story tools are on), the last 12 messages of your conversation with them, and your question. Never your story's passages, and never a key. Their answer is short, up to about 900 tokens. Where the provider can keep the start of a request (prompt caching, in Workshop → Providers), the part that never changes is kept and costs less. What each question cost is kept on this device and added up in Workshop → Providers, under "Saving money", as "the guide’s answers".
Making something

"Make something", at the foot of their panel, makes things with them: a character (a line or two from you, a few questions, and a draft you keep, take into the Studio or leave), a new opening for a card, a world, lore, a look over a card, a look over a story, a campaign, a preset, or a Binding (see "Making things with your guide"). Ask them to make one in words and their answer carries a button for it ("Make it", "Write the opening", "Make the world", "Write the lore", "Look it over", "Look over the story", "Set up the campaign", "Make the preset" or "Design the look"). With nothing asked yet, the starter questions end with "Make a character with me".
Looking pages up

With a model that can call tools, they can read any of their other pages ("Look up"), so one question can be up to three requests. Without tool calling they answers only from the pages they was sent, and says so when they are not enough.
What they keeps
Your conversation with them is kept on this device, the last 40 messages; a private window or cleared storage forgets it. Which tours you took or turned down is kept the same way.
Tours

Tours are scripted: no model is asked, so they work before you have a key (only "Your first story" sends anything, and only when you send your first line or ask for another take). They offers each once, by themself: the house when the welcome closes ("Show me around" or "Skip the tour"), then "Your first story", which sets out the starter set and goes on through the first session of the story it begins (see the starter set's page); a story's page, the map, a world and a campaign the first time you open each ("Show me", "Not now" or "Never offer tours"). The house tour's last step, at "?", names the other tours. An answered offer is remembered; leave the page without answering and it can come again. In a tour their card counts the steps ("3 of 12") and has "Back", "Next" ("Done" on the last) and "End the tour"; on a keyboard → goes on, ← goes back and Escape ends it. A step you do yourself waits until it is done, and offers "Do it for me". A step whose place is not on the screen is passed over; a place cut off at the edge (a row of buttons that scrolls sideways) is scrolled into view first. On a phone their card has "Hide": they steps aside to a small tab at the edge of the screen, the place still ringed, so you can read what is under them; a tap brings them back. Workshop → About has every tour again, "Offer a tour the first time I open something" and "Offer every tour again".

pages.title: Search and shortcuts
pages.summary: The command bar (Ctrl K, or ⌘K on a Mac) finds places, stories, cards, settings and actions; and every keyboard shortcut the app binds.

blocks.text: The command bar is one search box over the whole app. Ctrl+K opens and closes it (⌘K on a Mac; either modifier works), even while you type in a field. The rail's magnifying glass (tooltip "Search (Ctrl K)", or "Search (⌘K)" on a Mac) and the Aetheria medallion at the rail's top open it too; on a phone, "More", then "Search". Its field says "Go to a room, open a story or a card, find a setting…". It never asks a model anything.

Before you type it lists actions only (the "Do" group), ten at most, so inside a story "Show me around" appears only once you type. Places, stories, cards and settings appear only as you type. Results come in groups:

items: "Do": "New story", "Export this story" (inside a story: every chapter, as Markdown), "Go to Table", "Go to Stories", "Go to Library", "Make a character by interview", "Open Workshop", "Import…", "Keyboard shortcuts", "Ask your guide" (opens their panel) and "Show me around" (their tour of the house).
"Go": Table, Stories, Library, each deck ("Library · Characters", "Library · Presets"…) and "Studio · a character by interview".

"Open": stories by name (opening at the latest chapter; a story with several chapters also lists each as "Story · Chapter"), characters, lorebooks, worlds and presets. Unstarted stories and side scenes are left out.

"Workshop": every room ("Workshop · Providers"…) and single controls by their on-screen label, such as "Message sound", "Look for local models", "Check for updates" or "Export everything" (and "Worlds in stories", in Library · Worlds). Choosing a control opens its room, scrolls to it and rings it in gilt for a moment.
"Binding": the Bindings, each hinted "Wear" with its note. Choosing one wears it at once, a house Binding or another, as in Workshop → Appearance.

blocks.text: Names match first (a whole label, then its start, then a word in it, then anywhere in it), then a room's search words ("api key" finds Workshop · Providers); a description counts only when nothing matches by name. Up to 30 results, or "No match". It does not search passage text, lorebook entries or models. Inside it: ↑ and ↓ move, Enter goes, Escape closes.
Keyboard shortcuts (on a desktop)

Press ? (not while typing in a field) for the "Keyboard shortcuts" card, ? again to close it; the command bar's "Keyboard shortcuts" opens it too. The card lists what is bound. Ctrl means ⌘ on a Mac, and the card shows ⌘ there.

items: Anywhere: Ctrl+K the command bar; Ctrl+N a new blank story, opened at once; Ctrl+, the Workshop (at Appearance); Escape closes what is open, the top-most first.

In a story: Enter sends and Shift+Enter makes a new line (on a phone Enter makes a new line); Escape with nothing open stops a reply mid-sentence; Ctrl+C copies the passage under the pointer when no text is selected; Ctrl+O opens or closes the Observer; Ctrl+B folds or unfolds the Story Index; Ctrl+M voice mode on or off (in the desktop app).
Editing a passage: Ctrl+Enter saves, Escape cancels. Correcting a panel's value: Enter saves a line (Ctrl+Enter a list), Escape cancels.
The Library deck: ← and → move between cards, Enter opens one, Space chooses it (to read beneath the deck), F flips it.
Cards on the Table: arrows move a card (Shift, a little), Delete or Backspace takes it off, Enter opens it.
A preset's prompt chain: ↑ and ↓ on a block's grip move it; Enter or Space on a block chooses it.
A world map (click it first): V look around, E edit authored places, F fit the world, P find the party, arrows pan (Shift, further), + and − zoom, Escape clears the search and selection.
The world beside a story: Alt+M lets the world fill the view or puts it back; Alt+D, while it fills the view, clears everything else away.

blocks.text: Bound but not on the card: on the story map (when it lies across the screen) arrows pan, + and − zoom, 0 returns to where you are, and Enter on a passage reads it in the chat; in "New take with a note…" Ctrl+Enter writes the take and Escape cancels; with two or more characters in a story, @ in the composer offers their names (↑ ↓, Enter or Tab picks, Escape dismisses); Escape turns a flipped Library card back; menus take the arrows, Home and End; during a tour, → goes on, ← goes back and Escape ends it; in your guide's panel and the Observer's, Enter asks and Shift+Enter makes a new line.

pages.title: On a phone
pages.summary: On a phone or narrow window: the bottom bar and More, sheets you push down, Story tools, holding a passage, and swiping takes.

blocks.text: The phone layout is used in the Android app and in any window narrower than about 768 pixels, so a narrow desktop window looks like the phone.

The bottom bar replaces the rail: "Table", "Stories", "Library", "Workshop" and "More". "More" opens a sheet: under "This workspace", the current screen's index when it has one ("Story Index" in a story, "Sections" in a character, lorebook or preset editor and in the assembled request, "Workshop sections", "Drafts" in the Studio, "Stories" in Memory, "Models" when choosing a model); under "Tools & settings", "Search" (the command bar), "Import", "You" (who you play in the open story, and your personas; with no story open, your personas) and "your guide" (the guide: ask how anything works, or take a tour). Import is also in the Library's header.
Sheets

Side panes and pop-ups become sheets that rise from the bottom. Push one back down to close it (by the crest at its top: the Binding's mark between two short lines), tap outside it, or press ✕; a push down over something scrolled scrolls it back up instead. An index opens as a sheet from the left; push it back left to close it. Wherever there is an index (a story, an editor, the Workshop, the Studio), swiping in from the left edge of the screen opens it.

In a story the head has two labelled doors: "Index" (the Story Index) and "Tools", which opens the "Story tools" sheet (not the tools a story's model can use). It holds what the desktop head and composer carry: "Change model", "Assembled context" (the token count; opens the assembled request), "The story" (cast, chapters, notes), "Play a side scene…" (or "Back to the story" inside one) and "Observer". The Observer, and whatever you choose on the map, open in a sheet with "Details" and "Observer" tabs; the composer has no Observer button. On "Observer" the sheet stands at its full height, with the question box at its foot. The chevron folds the head away, the chapter strip starts folded, and the "Campaign" tab opens the journal as a sheet. Desktop only: the reply-cost estimate in the head, "Keep the world beside the story" and the inspector's World tab.
Passages

The buttons under a passage become "⋯". Tap it, or hold the passage for about half a second (a short buzz where the phone allows), for a menu: Copy, Edit, Speak (replies, and your own when "Read your passages in your character's voice" is on), Bookmark, "Remember this passage", More (the passage's More menu), Delete, and plugin actions.
Takes

The arrows under a reply ("2 of 3" on a phone, without the word "take") work as on a desktop, with bigger targets. Once a reply has two or more takes you can also swipe the reply: left for the next take (on the last take, a left swipe writes a new one: one request to the story's model), right for the previous (from the first it wraps to the last).
Writing

Enter starts a new line; the arrow at the right of the composer sends. While a reply is being written the arrow becomes a red stop button ("Stop writing"); a phone has no Escape, so that is how you stop a reply. While the on-screen keyboard is up, the app (and any open sheet) fits the part of the screen above it: the composer sits on the keyboard, growing upward as you write, and the bottom bar steps aside until the keyboard closes. In the Android app a field you tap scrolls into view. Composer and passage buttons and take swipes give a light haptic tap; there is no setting for it.

Elsewhere: the Table's buttons read "Continue", "Campaign" and "Begin" ("Opening", for "An opening from your guide", takes Continue's place while the bench can have one written), and its drawer opens from the "Archive drawer" bar ("Open", "Close"); Stories shows its shelves as tabs and a tap opens a story; the Library picks its deck from the title and has "Filter"; the Workshop has a "Sections" button; the story map is one column down the screen: scroll it (it does not drag), pinch it larger or smaller with two fingers, and tap a branch under its passage to open it in place; a world map zooms with two fingers, around the place between them.
What differs from the desktop:

items: "Check for updates" (Workshop → About) works only in the desktop app.

Voice mode (speaking your passages) is only in the desktop app: the Android app's commands have no "Turn voice mode on". The other way round, "Scan for lost conversations" (Workshop → Archive) works only in the Android app.
The Kokoro voice is not offered in the Android app, and "Reading width" is not shown on a phone.
Local models: on a phone "localhost" is the phone; give each server the computer's address on your network.
"Observer recall on this device" (Android app only) starts off, because indexing is expensive on a phone.
Keyboard shortcuts need a keyboard.

The Android app shows a one-time "Android WebView" notice if the phone cannot stream replies (it falls back by itself), and after a launch that did not finish starting, the next opens in "Recovery Mode".
